speechtext:

speechtext:
On April 30 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. 
Church) stated that he expected to be in a position to make a statement to the house with regard to the housing situation within a week. That is over two months ago. On June I I drew this matter to the attention of the minister, and he stated that he would comply with my request that the statement be expedited as much as possible. Another month has passed, and we have had no statement of government policy on this very important matter. May I urge upon the minister that he make a statement at the earliest possible opportunity.
At the same time I hope he will deal particularly with the difficult local housing situation in Ottawa, to which reference was made during the course of a debate in this house not so long ago, when I made the suggestion that some authority should be set up immediately to study the situation. Will the minister deal particularly with the suggestions which have been made regarding the construction of hostels?
I think this problem must be attended to, and government policy on both the larger matter and the particular matter should be made clear as soon as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I ought to mention to the house an incident which occurred to-day regarding which I feel very deeply, and as to which I should like to give the house such facts as I can.
I deeply regret to inform the house that two cadets of the officers' training centre at Brock-ville are in a very grave condition as a result of an accident which took place in the course of an exercise which the cadets were putting on here this afternoon. Part of the exercise was the crossing of the Rideau canal in battle order. These two cadets could not make the crossing and were rescued with considerable difficulty. When I left the scene only a few minutes ago resuscitation efforts were being continued, but up to that point without success, although all hope had not been abandoned. These two cadets are both noncommissioned officers recently returned from overseas to take their commissions.
Two other cadets were overcome in the crossing. They were taken to the hospital, and the report I have is that their condition is not serious. The names of the cadets are withheld pending receipt by the next of kin of notices which are being sent out in accordance with ihe regular practice.
I may say for the information of the house that two of the three officers in command of the party were officers who had come back from overseas for instructional work, including instructional work in battle drill.
I want to say further-this is information I got when I was on the scene-that all these cadets had been through this practice in water-crossing, only last week, and had practice of this kind as part of their regular training. The adjutant-general has already undertaken a thorough investigation, which will be made to-morrowT.

I am sure that we all join in the deepest sympathy for the next of kin, and I also feel that the cadets of the school should also have our sympathy and interest because they have entered most keenly and enthusiastically on exercises of this kind, which are regarded as a necessary part of the preparation for training in present-day warfare.

subsubtopic: PRESENT POSITION-MB. CHURCHILL'S STATEMENT IN BRITISH HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house no doubt will desire to have the latest word with respect to the battle of Egypt. I am not, unfortunately, in a position to give information based on official reports which have been received to-day, but through the courtesy of the Canadian Press I have received the Associated Press report of what was said by Mr. Churchill in the House of Commons to-day. In the course of his remarks Mr. Churchill said:
The battle of Egypt has brought the allies face to face with a disaster in the middle east equalled only by the fall of France, but the issue is not yet decided and "very considerable" reinforcements have reached or are approaching the battlefield.
Mr. Churchill also said:
Military misfortunes of the last fortnight in Cyrenaica and Egypt have completely transformed the situation, not only in that theatre but throughout the Mediterranean.
At any moment we may receive news of grave importance.
The press report states:
Mr. Churchill's sombre portrayal of the war in Africa was relieved only by his statement that "very considerable" reinforcements have reached or "are approaching" the battlefield.
And in indirect quotation:
I do not consider the struggle as in any way decided.
The Prime Minister also stated that the war, he thought, was likely to be a long one.
In that connection I should like to repeat what I said in the house the day after my return from Washington, as follows, as reported at page 3722 of Hansard:
There can be no doubt at all that the situation at the moment is one of the most critical with which the united nations have been faced, one of the most serious that has arisen in the course of the whole war. To get the true perspective one has, however, to recall the very critical situations which have arisen in the past, and to remind oneself that the forces of the united nations have been able to rise superior to any temporary reverse, and that to-day there can be no doubt that the united nations are stronger and better organized than they have been at

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, July 1, consideration of the motion of Hon. J. L. Usley (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the few years that I have been in this House of Commons I have heard many speeches-some good, some bad, some indifferent. Some speeches demanded this and that from the government; other speeches were very pleading; but the speech delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) on June 23, was the most "touching" speech ever delivered-in this house, in fact, ever delivered since confederation. I know that statement of mine will not be contradicted, because that speech and the effects of it will touch not only every taxpayer but everyone in Canada, and the coming generation as well. The taxes therein set out affect "rich man, poor man, beggar man, thief", and I can rightly say that if this rate of taxation continues for a few years there will not be any rich men in this country. To-day many men who are in the higher and the middle brackets have found that, in order to adjust themselves to these new taxes and the new modes of living they involve, they have to draw on their capital, and we can rest assured that if that state of affairs continues for a few years we shall have no rich in this country; there will be a wonderful levelling off process.
This budget has put a tax on practically everything in Canada except the air, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) has the power to put a ban on that with the defence of Canada regulations.

Yes, even a tax on your wife. And I might say that they do not value wives very highly, because we are only allowed $150 for them.
Through the defence of Canada regulations even the right of free speech is taken from us. To-day the people of Canada are not only taxed to death but restricted in every way, manner and form. With the defence of Canada regulations and the wartime prices and trade board, our people are virtually in straight-jackets. Some know it and some do not, but eventually they will. These wartime prices and trade board regulations are regulating the small business man out of business and are depressing the farmer so that he will be deeper in debt at the end of the war than he was before. In fact, the farmer is really the forgotten man, as I said in my budget speech of 1940. The Minister of Finance has gone very far this time because he has even taken the candy away from the babies and, by taxing' one-cent candy 30 per cent, candy which is the poor child's delight, he is taking away the extra nourishment that some of these children get, nourishment that is needed by them. I know he will find that the health of these children will be affected to a great extent. It will add to the work of the welfare societies and the children's aid societies throughout the country. I was quite pleased last night to hear just before the adjournment the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw) speak on nutrition, and I am sure he will agree with me that some children in the poorer families do need the extra nourishment from these one-cent candies. I have here a letter in which the writer says:
A great number of my customers are quite, concerned with the new 30 per cent tax on penny candies. With the increase on bulk candies, packages, chocolate bars, et cetera, it can be immediately added on, but with the penny line it cannot be raised so easily, for if it is made 30 per cent smaller there just won't be any candy left.
He goes on to say:
A young child who has done a few good deeds or helped his mother is very often rewarded with a penny and in 99 cases out of a 100 he goes to his favourite store to spend it on one-cent or some other confection. I am afraid that if he is deprived of this privilege there is nothing else in the world that will drive home in his mind the stern reality of war and its sacrifices, and surely none of us want these young children to have this brought upon them any sooner than it is necessary.
Some people might say that candy should be kept away from children. That is all right in some intances, if they are overloaded with it, but these poor children are not overloaded

with candy as some others are, and they should enjoy the right to have some candy. I think it would be proper for the minister to exempt this one cent candy and leave the tax on the higher priced confectionery, because otherwise the children's health will be affected.
As I listened to the Minister of Finance the other night delivering his budget speech, a story I read in the first book over forty years ago came back to me, the story of King Midas. Everything he touched, even his food, turned to gold. As the Minister of Finance ran his fingers through his golden locks, in the same breath he said that we expect a revenue this year of $1,481,000,000, or $609,000,000 more than last year; that is, more than half a billion dollars more than last year. It seems like a faiiy tale that Canada can raise that amount of money, but the Canadian people are willing and ready to pay it and will pay to the last cent without grumbling or maldng any row about the matter, so long as the government gives them a lead and economizes and stops waste in governmental activities. The people want the government to feel the pinch as much as they do, and it is only fair that they should have this feeling.
Yesterday I received an order for a return in regard to the Toronto Shipbuilding Company Limited, the former Dufferin Shipbuilding Company Limited, and Dufferin Paving and Crushed Stone Limited. The shipbuilding company is renting from the Dufferin company a 25-ton Kochning crane or derrick, a 20-ton crane, a 10-ton crane and two 71-ton cranes. The 25-ton crane is rented at $750 for the first shift per month, plus $375 for the second shift per month, or $1,125 a month. That crane, I believe, could be bought to-day, brand new, for $15,000, so that in a year the government will almost pay for it.

No; that is per month. The 20-ton crane is rented at $935 for the first shift and $470 for the second shift, or $1,405 a month. The 10-ton crane is rented at $565 for the first shift and $285 for the second, or $850 a month. The two 71-ton cranes, which operate on gasoline, are rented at $510 each for the first shift and $255 for the second shift, or $765 a month. The government paying the sum of $4,910 a month to this firm, the Dufferin Construction company, which I understand is run by the Franceschini outfit.
The other evening I was very much surprised to hear the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. O'Neill) speak of the wonderful work that

The Budget-Mr. Fraser (Peterborough)
the government is doing in turning out tanks and munitions of all kinds. He gave no credit at all to the people of Canada, and it is the Canadian people who are responsible for this production, not the government. The government had to be absolutely pushed into it by the opposition, who gave them the lead. Canada has done wonderful work in production. This dominion has done a good job, and the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) has also done a good job, but he can do a better job and so can we all. What we want is more production, and right away.
I have a few suggestions to make which I believe are constructive. To-day the Minister of Finance mentioned the National Housing Act, and I wish to refer to it because it is of vital importance at the present time to a great number of municipalities throughout Canada, especially Toronto, Peterborough, St. Catharines and Ottawa. What I am asking for- and I am sure the people in these municipalities are asking for it-is not only that this act be continued but that the government lend up to 90 per cent of the appraised value of all homes of 83,500 or less instead of just 90 per cent on homes of $2,500 as at present.
I have here a resolution which I am sure the Minister of Finance has already received:
City of Peterborough
City Clerk's office.
June 2, 1942.
Mr. G. K. Fraser, M.P.,
Parliament buildings,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Fraser:-
I beg to advise that the municipal council of the corporation of the city of Peterborough passed the following resolution at its meeting held last evening: -
"That whereas the housing situation in Peterborough is becoming more serious every day;
"And whereas it is the opinion of the council that this condition can be substantially alleviated by the continuation of the dominion housing loan facilities, particularly if a 10 per cent down payment requirement can be established;
Be it therefore resolved that this council petition the government of the Dominion of Canada, asking it to give serious consideration before deciding to suspend the provisions under the Dominion Housing Loan Act and, if possible, to extend the provisions whereby the 10 per cent down payment could be applied to homes of $3,500 and less; and that a copy of this resolution be sent to the Hon. J. L. Ilsley, Minister of Finance, and Mr. G. K. Fraser, M.P."
Yours sincerely,
E. A. Outram,
City Clerk.
I feel, and I know the people feel, that the workingmen of this country should be given a chance to build, to create, to have something to show for their work. Since the government
have lost less than one-half of one per cent on
this national housing plan there is no reason why it should not continue, because these homes are permanent, not temporary, makeshift affairs like those put up by Wartime Housing Limited. These war-time houses are supposed to be torn down within six months after the end of the war, and houses will be needed for these workers and other people to go into.
I was surprised to see in the paper the other day that the government had issued a permit, to the Ontario government evidently, to build a $50,000 home for the quints. That is not a right thing to do at this time. It will mean large upkeep; and if other people cannot afford it, or if the government does not want other people to spend money in that way, there is no reason why this residence should be built.
In regard to compulsory savings in connection with income tax, I am pleased that this has been brought in, but I believe that when the resolutions come before the committee of ways and means there will have to be many changes and clarifications in regard to this provision. I have here a letter from a real estate man, in which he says:
There is a point in the new budget under the compulsory savings plan which permits deductions up to a certain point when principal repayments are made under a registered mortgage. This seems clear enough.
However the budget has not apparently dealt with the payments of principal by purchasers of houses purchased under agreement of sale. This of course also includes those buying houses under the National Housing Act.
I have been to see one of the officials of our local income tax department, and they, too, are in doubt as to the interpretation of this item.
It would seem to me unfair and discriminatory to acknowledge the reduction of principal in the case of a registered mortgage, and to ignore the reduction of principal in the case of a purchase made un'der an agreement of sale. This latter reduction would affect far more workingmen than those reducing principal under a registered mortgage.
Then, under this compulsory savings tax, if a man wants deductions for his mortgage payments, his insurance or anything else, he has first to pay that amount to the government and then put in an application for refund, which may take months. That man would not only have to pay to the government but have to pay perhaps to the loan company also, a double payment. These people cannot afford that. Therefore the government should have some plan whereby cases like that could be checked monthly, so that there would be no hardship on the taxpayer. Take a doctor's account or a hospital bill for an operation; it might come to $200, which might be the full amount that the man is compelled to save by this new tax. When he pays that account and

The Budget[DOT]-Mr. Fraser (Peterborough)
produces that bill, automatically that should be taken off and should be allowed to extend over the full year, so that he would have nothing else to pay to the government. The receipt from the hospital or the doctor should be enough to cover the whole compulsory saving.
In connection with this-and I give this to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson) before he leaves the chamber-if the national revenue department would use some common sense and forget the red tape, I know perfectly well that this can be carried out, but you have to forget the red tape and use your brains, and then everything will be perfect.
In regard to insurance premiums, according to the budget they are to be allowed only on insurance already in effect. But what about a young couple getting married now or next week or next year? The young man will feel that he is not doing his duty unless he takes out life insurance to protect his wife and future family. Therefore I believe that insurance policies should be included even if they are taken out after this date. The Minister of Finance could draw up a schedule to take care of this, especially in the case of a small wage-earner, with an income of, say $2,000 and under, or $3,000 and under. Insurance policies of $1,000 or $2,000 that he might be allowed to take out should be included in this plan.
The same thing should be done with regard to victory bond purchases. There are many men and women in factories buying victory bonds by payments out of their wages to the company for which they work. Those payments also should be taken from this, compulsory saving. Otherwise they will have to lose their victory bonds; there is nothing else for it. I have one example of a man who has a salary of $2,000 a year; he pays $22 a month to the insurance company, $20 a month on the principal of a mortgage and, on top of that $40 rent. That makes $82 a month, or $984 a year. In addition to that, he will have to pay this new income tax, $215, of which $108 is compulsory saving. That makes $1,199 a year that this man has to lay out in fixed charges. If the government on top of that says he must pay his compulsory savings to the income tax branch at the end of the year, it will mean $1,307 he will have to lay out, leaving him only $693 to feed and clothe his family and for doctors, education, church, et cetera. That is for a man with a wife and two children. I believe men in that class should have a little better break, perhaps a little lower tax and a little better on the saving. This man would have less than $2 a day to keep his family, to build decent bodies on his children and put clothes on them. It

cannot be done. If he is compelled to pay that amount, it will mean just so much extra work for the welfare societies and the children's aid societies.
This year these welfare societies are going to feel the effect of this tax very severely, because people who up to now have made donations will have to cut down such donations from now on. They will not be able to help it, much as they would like to continue to contribute. So I think the government should make some provisions for these charities. Only this morning I met one gentleman who told me what his income was, what his tax would be, and the amount of his donations to various societies last year. If this year he donates one-quarter of the amount he gave last year, he will have to dip into his capital, which is very small. The same situation applies right across Canada. Every day these societies are doing more work; they are overloaded now. They are doing a great deal of the work of the dependents' allowance boards, and making a good job of it, and with all these war babies their work has been increased tremendously.
Under the compulsory saving provision, these savings are not required to be deducted from the. income of any person over sixty-five years of age, if that income is not in excess of $3,000. I believe that age limit should be reduced to sixty years, for many who reach sixty-five may never live to see sixty-six. For instance, I understand that in many municipalities female schoolteachers are retired at the age of sixty, and I also believe that in many businesses female workers are retired at the same age, so I believe this should be taken into account. In fact, I honestly believe that it will not be more than a few years until the Old Age Pensions Act is readjusted so that every man and woman in Canada over sixty years of age will receive not $20 a month but $40, which will not be charity but rather a refund on account of the taxes they have been paying all their lives.
Some lion. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
Do not applaud yet, because I have something to say which may hurt. In Canada the railways issue thousands of passes each year. I do not see why those who travel on passes, other than for business, should not be required to pay the 15 per cent tax on transportation. The wives of members of this house travel on passes. There is no reason why they should not pay the tax. Only yesterday, a railway man said to me, "I ride on this pass, and my wife rides on it, but Mrs. Jones next

The Budget-Mr. McLean
door, whose boy died in Thorold, had to pay a 15 per cent tax on the cost of her ticket, and she even had to borrow the money with which to buy the ticket." I believe that if this tax were collected on passes not used for business purposes, many dollars would be brought into the treasury, and it would act as a check on the number of passes being issued.
I believe we should start right here in the House of Commons, because "what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander".
A few weeks ago I heard an announcement over the radio on behalf of some finance company, whose name I have forgotten. It went something like this: "Why worry about your income tax? Why not let us look after it?" I believe the minister should see to it that these finance companies are not permitted to advertise in this way, because they only encourage people to spend their money. There must be a day of reckoning, and when that day comes, the people have to pay through the nose.	_
In conclusion, let me say that on the night of June 23, after the minister had delivered his budget speech, I met him entering the elevator outside this chamber. I said, "It must have taken a great deal of courage to make that speech." I do not know whether or not the minister agreed with me, though he shook his head as though to say he did not; but again I congratulate the minister upon his courage, because I know the people of Canada will congratulate him. The people are willing to pay; but for goodness sake let this government give us the lead in saving.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Almost all the speeches that have been delivered so far in this debate have dealt with the ways and means of raising money announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) in his budget speech. I am not going to refer to those ways and means, but I should like to make a few remarks with regard to the expenditure of some of the money that is to be raised by the methods announced by the minister. The great bulk of that money is for war purposes. I am not going to have anything to say about that, but I should like to refer to that very-much smaller portion of the money which is devoted to ordinary government expenditures that go on year after year.
War is a very wasteful business. War organizations are built up under conditions of great urgency. If sometimes the necessity of subordinating every other consideration to that of speed, in order to provide against a threat to our national existence, results in waste, there may be some grounds for excuse in connection with that waste but, no such grounds can be found for lack of the
strictest care in the expenditure of money for ordinary government purposes. On the contrary, the fact that by these very proposals we are taxing people high and low, rich and poor, to a degree that we have never before contemplated; the fact that many of the citizens of our country have been or before the end of the war will be compelled to modify their standard of living very materially in order to meet our taxation demands, makes it imperative that the care which should be exercised at all times by those charged with the responsibility of spending public funds should be intensified fourfold in time of war.
In at least some departments of government I submit that this is not being done.
I am not going to range over the whole field of government expenditure, of course, and I hope that I may not give any grounds for being accused of vague and ineffective generalizations, such as those with which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) was charged,
I think quite properly, by the Minister of Finance some six weeks ago, when the first supply bill was under discussion. In fact, I shall be painfully specific. I make one submission, and one only, based upon my obesrva-tions during six or seven years in this house.
I submit that there is due; there is past due; and, in fact, there is long past due a drastic curtailment in the cost of government services here in Ottawa. I shall confine myself to still narrower limits; I shall confine myself to only a small branch of the service in Ottawa, namely, the legislation branch.
We are dealing with thousands of millions of dollars and I know I am winning the danger of creating the impression that I am one of those men with a small mind who can deal only with small matters, who cannot see^ the large items, who can see only the petty things. It may be that some hon. members will be impatient and ask: When we are dealing with a budget of hundreds of millions of dollars, why spend time in discussing a comparatively small matter? My answer is that often there is a danger that in looking at the forest one is so blinded that he cannot see the trees. These vast sums of money that are being raised and spent are, in the last analysis, made up of small items. Any attempt to bring about economies will be absolutely futile if we remain up in the clouds, if we deal only with generalities and refuse to come down to earth to discuss the details of the smaller items which inevitably make up the larger totals. As I say, I am limiting myself to a small branch of the government service, but I do not say that what I have to say about this branch is not true in a greater or lesser degree of the
The Budget-Mr. McLean

other larger departments in Ottawa. What I have to say about this branch will occupy all the time I feel free to take.
In connection with this department there is costly and unnecessary duplication and indefensible overstaffing. There is lack of businesslike organization. There exists the vicious practice of nepotism which is so destructive of morale, efficiency and cooperation. There is waste of material, waste of man-power and waste of woman-power. Some of the salaries paid are entirely out of proportion to the qualifications required and the nature of the services rendered. There is lack of supervision and direction which should correct these abuses. I shall give [DOT] a few examples of duplication.
In the basement of this building there is a post office for the House of Commons equipped with a permanent staff. Close to it in the same basement there is another post office for the other house. On this floor there is the House of Commons reading room, staffed with permanent officials and supplied with magazines and newspapers; there is a duplicate for the other house, similarly staffed and equipped. In the basement there is a stationery distribution room for the House of Commons with a full-time staff; there is a duplicate for the other house. In the basement there is an accountant's office for the House of Commons with a full-time staff; there is a duplicate for the other house. If we want to get down to really small things, we find that there is a barber shop in the basement for this house and a duplicate for the other house. These are just a few of the costly and unnecessary duplications that come to my mind. It may be argued that these duplications are unavoidable, but I submit that even if they were unavoidable the cost of the services are unnecessarily expensive and some of the services cannot be justified at all.
Let me give an example in connection with the reading room. The House of Commons reading room is a most convenient luxury, but it is used very little. It is open only while the house is in session and is not open to the public at all. It is used by only a few members. Go into the reading room of the House of Commons and you will find a much larger number of the paid staff of the house there during working hours than you will members of parliament. This is just another evidence of my charge of overstaffing. The salaries paid to the staff amount to $8,780, and the cost of the magazines, periodicals and newspapers is $3,800. This item for the other house amounts to $2,500, which gives a total for the two reading rooms of over $15,000 a year. We have a magnificent parliamentary

library with salaries paid amounting to about $55,000 a year. Can any hon. member defend the retention of the two reading rooms at a cost of $15,000 a year?
I am giving figures to be put on the record, some of which will probably be challenged. I do not guarantee that they are correct for to-day or yesterday or a month ago. It is not easy to keep these figures up to date. It may be said that such and such an officer has retired, that a certain position has not been filled, but my answer will be to turn to the estimates before the house and say that no such reductions are reflected in them.
The post offices are not under the Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock) as they ought to be; they are under the legislation branch. There has been some reduction in this particular service. About a year and a half ago protests were made about the staff of nineteen handling the mail for this house, and the staff was reduced by six. At the present time I believe there are eight permanent employees and five sessional employees, employed at a cost of between $19,000 and $20,000 a year. If these two post offices were amalgamated, put under the Postmaster General and handled in the efficient and economical way that post offices throughout the country are handled, I feel sure that this cost would be cut in two.
As I say, there is the stationery room for the House of Commons and another one for the Senate. Surely that is a stupid idea. The salary list for these two offices amounts to $11,256 a year. This is to pay a staff to handle the requisitioning, storing and distributing of stationery. The cost of stationery for the House of Commons is $35,000 a year; the same item for the Senate is $9,000, making a total, including salaries, of $55,000. This one branch needs looking into most carefully. In the stationery branch of the House of Commons there is an inventory of some $40,000, made up of articles numbering about 1,200. A large number of those articles ought not to be there at all. The waste in. stationery is simply shocking.
I am sure hon. members are familiar with the wasteful attitude of the staff of this house in connection with stationery. This may seem a small item, but it is indicative of an attitude that must be corrected. These wasteful methods would not be tolerated in private business for one day, and they should ' not be tolerated here.
A fruitful source of waste is the lack of modern, businesslike organization in the branches. I realize that as soon as you try to

The Budget-Mr. McLean
correct this you will be confronted with traditional methods and attitudes that will be most difficult to change and correct. _ The very architecture of the buildings is an obstacle, but not an insuperable one.
I am sure members have noticed that there is on the part of a great many civil servants and officials a tendency to make their own office the centre of a distinct organization, with a secretary, a stenographer, a messenger and so on. I do not want to detract from the dignity or the prestige of any civil servant or of any official, but I suggest that that dignity be consistent with modern ideas of efficiency and economy.
Again, let me be quite definite. Let me give an example. One group of the offices of this house, of which there are many-and I will take the offices with whom the members are most familiar, the offices that are closest to this house-consists of that of the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker, the Clerk, the Assistant Clerk and the Sergeant-at-Arms. The functions of these officers are closely related, and any private organization having officers whose functions were similarly related would have their offices together. I doubt very much if in any private organization they would all have separate offices, but even if they did they would be grouped together and would have a common staff. But what have we here? _
I am not suggesting for a moment that this is a condition which is only a present condition; it is a condition which my investigation into the records shows has gone on for thirty or forty years. Let us look at these offices. The staff of these five officers of the house consists or did consist last year or the year before-I do not know what they are at the present moment-of six secretaries, a stenographer, a steward and a messenger. The salary cost to the country was S22,600 a year. This does not include the sessional staff; it does not include assistance from the stenographers of the sessional staff or of the messengers of the sessional staff, who are available to these officers. These are the salaries of the staff which are paid all the year round to people whose duties are confined entirely or almost entirely to the offices of these officers of the house.
I could go on and give other examples in connection with other offices and groups of offices scattered under this roof.
I want to say just a word or two about the sessional staff of stenographers. I have only time to touch on a very few items which come to my mind. We have a staff of sessional stenographers numbering 129. That staff was reduced this year by about thirteen. There is a great lack of supervision and direction of the work of that staff. A great
many of these stenographers, as members know very well, work very hard and efficiently. Some of them do the work of three or four or five members. But I will assert without fear of contradiction that there is extreme unfairness in connection with the distribution of the work. If that work were properly and fairly distributed, we could cut out one-third of these stenographers, with a saving of thousands of dollars to the country, and with a great deal better feeling among members of the staff.
Take the messengers. I do not suggest for one moment that any efficient organization should not have a sufficient number of messengers to facilitate its work; but let me point out that while we are sitting here during the session there are employed on the messenger staff, in temporary or permanent capacities, forty-eight employees and, when the house adjourns, thirty remain on the staff all through the year. The total cost of this messenger service is 864,500 a year. Is it not a fact that either one of two things is true: Either half of these men are sitting down doing nothing but drawing their pay, or else they are engaged in work for which we have no right to ask the public to pay. I think a great many members will say that both these things are true.
I said there was nepotism. In Ontario, if one member of a family is engaged in the service of the province, no other member of that family is permitted to be engaged in the provincial service. I do not suggest for one moment that we should go to anything like that length, but I do say that nepotism is a pernicious system. It is destructive of cooperation; it is destructive of efficiency, and no officer, high or low, should be permitted to have in his office under him a son or daughter or brother or sister. But that is practised here, and it should end and end at once.
I mentioned something about salaries but I cannot take the time to deal with that at any length. When I speak of salaries I do not wish to be misunderstood. I am not one of those who object to high salaries. We have some men in the employ of the government ' who are paid what would be considered high salaries, but in my estimation those men would be cheap if they were paid twice the amount. We have members of the cabinet who, in my opinion, would be cheap if we paid twice what we are paying them. But if members will closely examine the salaries that are paid here in Ottawa and consider the qualifications required and the services rendered, they will find some very grave defects.
I have this further to say about salaries. I am making what may be considered a reckless statement but I am making it deliber-
The Budget-Mr. McLean

ately. There are in our employ under this roof men whose salaries run between $3,000 and $4,000 a year whose work, measured by the performance of similarly qualified men in private industry or commerce, or in any well-ordered municipal office in our towns, spread over the working days of the year, would not amount to two hours' work a day, and some members have said to me that I would be nearer the mark if I said one hour a day. There was a time when there were positions that were called sinecures, and we sort of took them as a necessary evil, but in these days, Mr. Speaker, sinecures should be out, and out for good.
I suggest that in this one comparatively small department of which I am speaking, $150,000 a year would be a very, very conservative estimate of what could be saved if we exercised the same care in the supervision of the work of this branch that any member would exercise in his own private business.
I think the members will recognize that it is not a pleasant task that I have undertaken this afternoon. I do not like making this kind of speech. I am not fond of making speeches at all. I think this is the second speech I have made in six years, but I know from my conversation with a good many members that they feel just as keenly about this as I do. My practice has been, whenever I saw what I thought were abuses, not to air them on the floor, but first to go to the minister concerned, or preferably to the officer or official concerned, and in that practice I have had considerable success. I have followed the same, reasonable, decent procedure for the last two years in connection with this matter, with indifferent success. I am now bringing it to the attention of the house because I want the support of hon. members who feel the way I do; I want the support of hon. members who, perhaps, have not looked into these things as they might, in order to bring about a state of feeling whereby this blot on our government service can be corrected. I am not making an attack on the government, or, particularly, on this parliament.

speechtext: It is on the system.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) says, it is on the system which has been going on as long as I can find in the records. It is the system I want to see changed. This is not an attack on the administration. Certainly the last thing I would have in mind would be to criticize the Minister of Finance. There are things that should be changed, and to do so will require the support of hon. members 
of all parties. I must say-and I do so in all kindness to my friends of the opposition, from whom I have received nothing but kindness, that the indifference with which they have viewed what has been going on, as their leader said the other day, under their very noses-though he was indefinite-fills me with amazement.
Do not misunderstand me. I do not say that it is not the duty of a government supporter to bring these matters to light. It is. But surely it is a duty of the opposition. What is the opposition for? They know these things have been going on. They were going on when my hon. friends opposite were in power. Some hon. members now in opposition filled cabinet positions, and one, Mr. Speaker, occupied the honourable position which you hold. I have waited for years; I have looked at members of the official opposition, business men who know what efficiency means in business and understand the necessity of it, some of them have sat in this house continuously for twenty years or more, and never once have I heard any one of them attack this waste and these abuses which have been going on for years and years.
I am a great believer in the system of a government and an opposition. But the successful working of that system presupposes an industrious and alert opposition. We have heard a great deal about complacency, lack of leadership. I think we have had complacency deep and slumberous for years, complacency on the part of the opposition in refusing to say a word about these abuses.
I do not want to say anything unkind. I know that the leader of the opposition is filling a difficult position. Perhaps it is rather unfortunate that he does not happen to be the gentleman who, if and when his party comes into power, will place men in cabinet positions, because that would give him a little more disciplinary power; he would be able to issue orders to his followers and put them to work at this, that and the other task which he knows very well should be done and is not being done.
As for my hon. friends further to the left, I have heard them on one or two occasions single out some salary of $15,000 or $20,000 or $30,000 for a very ineffective attack, without giving grounds for it. But we have heard nothing from them on this matter, perhaps because of that magic system by which they are able to pull money out of the blue like rabbits out of a hat; apparently it does not matter much to them what is spent. But my hon. friends of the official opposition do not hold these views; they have not been

The Budget-Mr. McLean
bewitched by the oratory of our hon. friends to the far left. Like myself, they realize that when the government imposes taxation, in the last resort the money is paid for by the sweat of the brow of people high and low throughout the country, or else out of savings which have been earned by the sweat of their brow and have been accumulated by habits of frugality and thrift.
My only motive in speaking to my opposition friends is that I want their support. I want the support of all hon. members, and I believe that nobody will be more pleased to have it than the man who to-day occupies the position of Minister of Finance. I feel the more free to speak as I have done because I have the utmost confidence that in the Minister of Finance we have a man who feels keenly about these matters, perhaps more keenly than any other man in the house, and I do not think for one moment that he will resent the criticisms and suggestions I have made this afternoon. Probably no man in many years has risen so rapidly as he has in the estimation of the people as a man of courage, a man who has his feet on the ground and who is doing a wonderful job in the Department of Finance; and it is in order to help him in the good work he is doing that I am bringing these matters before the house.
I do not want it to be supposed that I am making an attack on the civil service. I am not. I am simply trying to remove what they know much better than I do is an impediment to them in their progress to the highest and best in the profession to which they have given their lives. I want to pay tribute to our civil service. I am never done telling service clubs and others whom I address that the civil service of Canada is second to none. I know the Minister of Finance and other ministers have men of the very highest ability and devotion to duty in their departments. Many of them are working long hours and are not limiting themselves to their ordinary duties, but are giving themselves unstintedly to war work. We have a civil service of which we may be proud. It is no reflection on and no criticism of them that we remove the deadwood that is clogging their progress and sapping the strength of the organization to which they belong. "Dead* wood" is the word. You know the effect of deadwood on an otherwise healthy tree. If some tree like an elm has a branch which dies, it may remain for many years and it does not hurt the tree a bit. But let a branch of a hard maple die; in a very short time it becomes dozy and forms a channel through which rain and frost and heat and insects
and fungi enter the trunk, the heart of that tree; rot sets in at the heart, and the tree becomes weakened and dies. But the careful husbandman, as soon as that branch dies, will cut it off clean and close to the trunk, so that the healing processes of the inner bark will very quickly spread a living layer of clean, fresh wood over that wound, until hardly a scar is left. That is all I am asking to be done with the civil service.
I was discussing a very small branch of the service, namely the legislation branch; but I am not suggesting for a minute that the conditions I have described do not apply to other and much larger departments, such as public works, agriculture, the post office, mines and resources, national revenue, the Department of the Secretary of State and so on, with their hundreds of offices and their thousands upon thousands of employees. I am not going to make any categorical statements regarding them, because I have not here any definite information to substantiate anything I may say. But if we were to go through these departments and examine them as we examined this one, I doubt whether any hon. member would be so optimistic as to think that the conditions I have described here do not obtain in greater or lesser degree throughout these departments.
Now is the time when we ought to correct this situation. While we were paying millions of dollars in unemployment money, it might have been said that the time was not opportune to turn people out of their jobs; but to-day we are building up organizations with thousands of employees, and if there is overstaffing and waste of man-power and woman-power, the natural thing to do is to work these people into these other organizations that are being built up temporarily. Now is the psychological time to do so. As I have said, these things are hard to correct, but I am quite sure that the civil service generally is not of a state of mind different from that of the rest of the people, and by taking steps to bring about this reform now I am sure we would find them responsive and ready to give such cooperation as would be impossible at any other time.
My time is up. I was going to make some suggestions as to how we ought to set about correcting the situation. Corrected it ought to be, and1 corrected without delay. My time will not permit me to make these suggestions, but I will say this. I hope no one thinks I would suggest something that was suggested some years ago, that in order to cut down overstaffing we should employ another large highly paid staff of experts, civil servants, to go through these departments and tell us what
The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis

ought to be done. I throw out this hint, that if there are not among the private members of the house men of business experience, men with a sense of responsibility to the taxpayers in their ridings, men with ability who could be of assistance in this work, then our people have picked the wrong persons to represent them as members of parliament.
Mr. ANGUS MaeINNIS (Vancouver East): We have all listened with interest to the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. McLean). He spoke about small things, but in the aggregate they are not unimportant. I do not suppose that any member of this house, particularly if he comes here with a background similar to mine and maybe also that of the hon. member, being brought up in the hard way, taught to turn a copper over two or three times before we decided to spend it, will fail to appreciate what the hon. member has said. Personally I hate to throw away a sheet of paper unless both sides of it have been used. The condition to which the hon. member has referred can be rectified, but it can be rectified only if members are prepared to allow the administration to undertake the work without bringing pressure to bear when some individual is interfered with. This is the first thing that has to be recognized, and in the last analysis improvement in the matters will depend upon the members of the house. The situation here is a tradition that has developed out of the beginnings of our parliamentary institutions, when parliament was considered to be the best club in the country, a place where gentlemen met to talk over the affairs of the nation and not to do anything much in particular, with a staff of servants to wait on them. That day is past. Parliament to-day is a huge administrative establishment, and it should be run on that basis.
In saying a few words on the budget, I wish first, in common with members who have already spoken, to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) upon his performance of a very difficult task. I hope the minister will not take any criticism I make as indicating a lack of appreciation of the time, the thought or the study he has put into the preparation of the budget. I hope he will not take any criticism I make as a doubting of his sincerity in wishing to deal equitably with all concerned.
This is of necessity a war-time budget. The minister was dealing with Canadian conditions as affected by our war activities. The economic consequences of the war are more keenly realized now than they were in 1940 or 1941. The minister had, therefore, two main tasks before him in preparing his budget: first, to find money to meet the costs of the war, and,

second, to prevent prices from rising by taking money out of the pockets of consumers about as fast as it gets there. Whether we like it or not, this last point has to be recognized, and the importance of it can be realized from the answer to a question in the house on June 17. The question was asked by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Kirk) as to what amount of money was in circulation in Canada as at March 31 for each of the years from 1929 to 1942, both inclusive, and what was the amount of the same, per capita, during each of the above-mentioned periods. This can be found at page 3407 of Hansard. I will not repeat all the figures given. I will give them for two or three years. At March 31, 1929, the amount of money in circulation was a little over $222,000,000, and the per capita amount of circulating media in the hands of the public was $22.21. At the depth of the depression, March 31, 1932, the total amount of circulating media in the hands of the public was a little over $176,000,000, and the per capita amount was $16.77. At March 31, 1939, the total amount of circulating media in the hands of the public was almost $236,000,000, and the per capita amount was $20.85. This was the last pre-war month given in the statement. On March 31, 1942, the total amount of circulating media in the hands of the public was almost $523,000,000, with a per capita circulation of $45.79. During the depression there is no doubt there was a shortage of money in circulation as compared with the goods available. I shall not go into the reasons for that now; they are obvious. The money that has now come into circulation came in because of increased production. War production, that is the production of war goods, is increasing, and the production of consumers' goods is decreasing. In view of this condition, it is the height of folly to suggest that the production of consumers' goods can be increased so as to raise the over-all living standards of the people during the war. Later I will come to a point which I think should be made in this connection.
I believe, however, there is a third task which the minister did not undertake. Possibly it does not come altogether within his department; it may come under a number of departments, but the financial planning for it would have to be done by the Department of Finance. This third task would be planning to utilize the services of everyone in essential production of either war or ordinary consumers' goods, with only luxury production excluded.

What I want to point out is that we should not penalize people for raising a family. Walter Nash, in an address made in Ottawa recently, told us of the mothers' allowances
act in New Zealand, which has been in effect I think since the Labour party came into office, although I am not sure of that, and which provides that if the family income falls below
The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis

a certain amount, the state pays directly to the mother a stated amount per child. Mr. Nash said that because of that provision the birth rate in New Zealand had increased by some four points since the time the legislation came into effect.
As I said before, I am not complaining about the effect of the income tax on single persons or married persons without children, or even married persons with one child, but we should be careful not to allow the income tax to reduce family incomes unduly. I have heard statements in the house on occasions that corporations might have to draw on their capital. If the family income is unduly reduced, the family also may be compelled to draw on its capital, and its capital is the health of the family. I should1 like to impress that point upon the minister. There is also the fact that it costs more to keep children at certain ages, particularly when they are fourteen, fifteen and sixteen, when they are going to high school or perhaps to university. Sometimes it becomes very difficult to keep children at school because the parents cannot give them any spending money, which I think members will agree is not a good thing.
There is something else in the budget I should like to bring to the attention of the house. Section 13 of the Income War Tax Act provides for the taxation of the undistributed profits of corporations in the hands of the shareholders or set aside for the shareholders. I do not know whether this section of the act is being applied; my impression is that it is not.

speechtext: Not very much. I can remember one case in which it was applied, but that is about all.

In any event I believe the minister should take into consideration the freezing of these surpluses as of August 31, 1939, or some other date, and that all increases since that time be taxed as personal income.
I wish to commend the minister for having introduced the principle of deducting the income tax at the source. I believe this will make it much easier for persons with small incomes, who because of necessity live very close to the limit of their incomes, so that at the end of the year there is very little, if anything, set aside to take care of the payment of a lump sum. I would suggest also that some method be found to provide that too many deductions are not made from the pay envelope at the same time. Because of unemployment insurance contributions and other contributions, a great many deductions are made from the pay envelopes of the workers these days. Those who recall the trouble at Arvida last

year will remember that one cause of that trouble was the deductions which were made on a certain date, without the employees having been notified that such deductions were to be made.
In this regard I would suggest to the minister that the pressure and coercion in connection with the buying of war savings certificates should be discontinued, particularly in the case of persons receiving low incomes. In this connection I have in my hand letters which passed between an employer and an employee, which reveal a situation that in my opinion is nothing less than scandalous. We have heard in this house some strong opposition to the conscription of wealth. I am going to read something that will show conscription of wealth with a vengeance; compulsory conscription of wealth, as applied to a wage-earner. First, I have a letter signed by the general manager of the Canadian Western Lumber Company, Limited, Fraser Mills, British Columbia. I imagine this was a form letter sent to all the employees of that company, since the name of the employee and his clock number are typed in, while the rest of the letter is a carbon copy. I am not going to read the1 whole letter; this is the important paragraph:
The minister-
That is, the Minister of Finance.
-has issued instructions to all employers that they must contact each employee personally, and, as far as possible insist on their subscribing to this scheme, but I am quite sure you do not want any undue pressure made in order to have you join in a voluntary way.
Can anyone harmonize "undue pressure" or pressure of any kind with voluntary action? Well, one employee wrote back to say that he was not buying war savings certificates, and later on I will give the house his reason. He was sent another letter, and he replied once more saying that he was not going to buy them. Finally, on April 25, 1942, this letter was addressed to the employee, Mr. T. Hebert, clock No. 1698.
Fraser Mills, B.C.

I have for acknowledgment your letter of April 20 in further reference to war savings certificates.

Seemingly, the "undue pressure" for voluntary participation worked satisfactorily.
We have now received instructions from the president of the company that owing to the Minister of Finance having made it abundantly clear that it is the duty of employers to see that all employees subscribe, we are obliged to see that these instructions are carried out.

The above-mentioned received to-day. In reply I beg to inform you that I intend to carry on as I have been doing, by giving financial assistance in the war efforts as I see fit best. . . .
But as for me to buy war savings certificates, not for a long time to come, because it would be capitalizing on the lives of the boys in the army, including my own boy. . . .
From the tone of your letter above-mentioned, it sounds to me as if Hitler had dictated the letter, at least it's tactics that was used by his storm troopers for nazi propaganda, and I always understood that the war was for the purpose of destroying such principle of interference in the private lives of the citizens of the country. Apparently it is being applied in this country.
Unless I hear from you before five p.m., April 30, 1942, I will punch the clock for the last time, after seventeen years, four months and five days of continuous service. . . .
This man has the courage of his convictions, for he adds:
Please have my pay cheque ready for me at that time.

In case of the possibility of my reinstatement to my former position, I wish to make this point clear for you in case it might come up in the discussions. As I left the job for the principle of freedom of action, I will go back on the same job when the imposition in dispute is lifted, as I have handled that job for seventeen years, four months and five days. I still can do it again. . . .
You can coerce people who are not much good, people without spirit; but it is the man who will not follow the crowd, the man with some spirit, who has to take the rap. I think coercion in this connection should stop.
I mentioned conscription of wealth, and I should like to say a word or two about that. Until this budget came down, evidently no one knew what conscription of wealth was, but the moment it came down they recognized what they had not known immediately. This budget is not conscription of wealth as we understand that term. I do not think I can do better than to read to the house some paragraphs from a speech made by Sir Richard Acland, an outstanding
Liberal in the British House of Commons. Speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the throne on November 12, 1941, he said:
We are to have a debate on production. I wonder whether in that debate anybody will mention the root cause of the difficulty. The root cause does not lie in ministerial incompetence, or in absenteeism, or in managerial inefficiency, or in the overlapping of departments, or anything of that kind. It lies in the fact that you are trying to get the maximum production of the whole, through the instrumentality of men who must have one eye resting on the post-war capital value of the particular part which they control. I want to keep a sense of proportion. I am not for one moment supporting those exaggerated statements which hold up every shareholder as being a conscious and deliberate saboteur of the war effort for his own individual cash benefit. Of course not. But there is an association of ideas in the minds of those who take for granted that the old system will go on after the war which leads to a conflict of interest altogether too great to be tolerated throughout a long war. It may not matter if there is to be a collapse of Germany in twelve months, but it does matter in a long war.
Let hon. members think of these points. It is in our interest to postpone every postponable repair; it is in the interests of the owners to get every repair done and have it charged up to the excess profits tax. It is in our interest to work the good seams in the coal mines now; it is in the owners' interests to postpone work on the good seams until after the war. It is in our interest to share trade secrets; it is in the owners' interests to preserve them. It is in our interest to concentrate output in every factory on one or few products; it is in their interests to keep the factory flexible by making as many different products as possible. It is in our interest that skilled men should spend part of their time teaching their skill to unskilled men; it is in the owners' interests that skilled men should be kept on direct production all the time. It is in our interest to save paper by cutting down advertising; it is in their interests to spend money which belongs to us-because otherwise it would go in excess profits tax-in advertising things like aeroplane parts.
That is what we consider as conscription of wealth. The government of this country should direct, for the purpose of winning the war, the resources of the country without interference from private owners.
About a week ago when I was absent from the house-I think I have lost two days since the session began, and that was one of them- mention was made of the Japanese evacuation from the coastal area. The only reason why I mention this matter now is that I would have spoken at that time had I been here. Possibly before the session ends, although I am not hoping for it, I may have occasion to differ from and disagree with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). Therefore I want to say now that I think his department has handled a most difficult job in an efficient

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis

manner. The removal of the Japanese is one of the biggest war jobs that any department has had to handle since the war began. We uprooted and removed a population of nearly 25,000 people. Someone referred to it in a letter to me as the "expulsion of the Acadians". The removal of these people began in a strained atmosphere with a population that was almost hysterical, sniping at those carrying out the operation.
The point that should be remembered is that a great many of these people are Canadian citizens no matter what the colour of their skins may be, and they are entitled to the treatment that would be accorded to a Canadian citizen whose skin is white. We should also keep in mind that when the war is over, we shall have to continue to live with these people, as we shall have to continue to live with our enemy nations unless we are going to be continually at war. This is not a British Columbia problem alone. The people of the other provinces should have recognized this as a national problem and been more cooperative. They are coming somewhat .to their senses, and I hope the matter will be adjusted from now on.
I should like to draw attention to the unreasonable lengths the Canadian people have gone in their treatment of Canadian-born persons of Japanese origin.
