Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance, (Mr. Ilsley) has presented to parliament a budget more extensive in scope than any other budget that has ever been presented to this house. This is necessitated by the grave and difficult times through which we are passing. I am sure it will bring a realization to the people of this dominion of the magnitude of the task that lies ahead and the gravity of the crisis in which we find ourselves. Reference was made to that by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and1 indeed every day we receive news of ever-increasing gravity which should make us all ready to shoulder the burdens and sacrifices and obligations involved in this budget. But I do feel, Mr. Speaker, that as the people of Canada accept the tremendous burdens which this budget imposes, they should have full confidence that the vast machinery of government which we are now creating will be our servant instead of our master; for otherwise the morale necessary to achieve victory will not be sustained.
In that event I am sure we can make a total war effort in this country and meet all the obligations which this budget imposes, though sometimes it seems that it will take all the vast resources of this dominion, of the factory, of the farm and every other productive facility, to meet the great challenge that is now ours. It is true that the effort we shall make will not actually consume all this tremendous store of wealth, but this budget and the other necessary measures that will be brought down to provide the money required will encumber the vast resources of this country and place an open-end mortgage upon them, the extent of which can scarcely be appreciated yet, and the maturity of which is indeed unknown. It is not a mortgage
44561-245 J
on any particular government, but a mortgage on the Canadian people, that we must assume. A gigantic task lies before us.
Before dealing briefly with the ways and means proposed in this budget for raising the amount of money required, I feel we must consider the purposes for which we are raising the money, and that is the maintenance of the productive capacity of this dominion. In that connection I wish to refer to one particular phase of production which I think is in jeopardy at the present time, namely, our agricultural production. It is not in any spirit of pleading for a particular class of people, or of emphasizing equality of service and sacrifice, that I say that the farmer in this country has been the one who has been more or less forgotten. It is most essential, viewing the broad picture, that we have a planned economy and that we maintain our productive capacity as a vital necessity for the war.
Some time ago, Mr. Speaker, I advocated in this house that we should establish a food production committee for farm products. It is true that we have many special committees at work now, but I have long felt that we should establish a food production committee, representative of producers from all the different parts of this dominion and of consumers as well, to meet the challenge that is flung to-day at the great basic industry of agriculture. I would again urge upon the government that even at this late day they give careful consideration to the establishment of such a food production committee. No longer can we leave the agricultural economy of this dominion in a haphazard condition. It must be organized for the future and planned now, if we are to meet the requirements of the war and what will follow the war.
I do not believe that we shall cope successfully with this important aspect of our war effort by the hand-to-mouth policy which has been followed thus far. It seems to be a month-to-month policy to face a year-to-year war obligation. We have our own troops to feed; we shall have to send much more food to Britain as the years pass. We have been told to-day that we are facing a long war, and there is not one of us who is now so optimistic as to believe that victory can be won in a short time. We must at once do some long-range planning. We must organize the agricultural economy of this dominion on a basis which will create more certainty and less uncertainty for the producer. If I were to apply the term "equality of sacrifice" to any one class, as working harder than another, I know there is not an hon. member within sound of my voice who knows anything about the farm-
The Budget-Mr. Rowe

ing communities of this dominion, whether i Quebec or Ontario or the west, but will agrf that no class of our people is struggling hardt and enduring more difficulty, so far as securin help is concerned, than the farmers. The>
have to compete against the higher pricer which are offered for labour in manufacturing plants-all essential, it is true, to our effort But I do feel that the government must give careful consideration to the position in which the farmer finds himself to-day. I know many farmers who are paying at least twice as much for hired help as they paid prior to the war.
It is true that the prices of some of the commodities the farmers are selling have risen to some extent. I am not pleading that the farmer should make a lot of money out of the war. Neither is he. He is waiting, he is willing, he is desirous of giving his war service at home, as his boys are giving them overseas. He is not asking for a large profit, but merely for the assurance of some security, for the opportunity-which I submit he has not now -to make both ends meet. It is all very well to say that he should carry on with production from the point of view of patriotism and loyalty. There is not a more loyal and patriotic class of people than those who inhabit the open spaces of this country, and who by the nature of their toil have the time and opportunity to meditate upon the issues involved.
Very little consideration has been given to the position in which the farmers found themselves when this war began. We have seen no sign of a plan to rehabilitate the farmer after the period of low prices so that the needed production may be had when prices are somewhat higher. The farmer has been the victim of periods of deflation, and he is now to be the martyr of a period of inflation. In view of the fact that ceiling prices have been placed on the products he has to sell, without any ceiling on the cost of the labour he has to buy, is it any wonder he feels he is being asked to produce more for less?	.
Some may say that the ceiling is placed higher than the prices of some years ago. To my mind that is only an empty gesture, and is so understood by practically every farmer. He pays one hundred per cent more for his labour; he finds a ceiling price is put on the products he has for sale-and he is singled out in that respect. Not only that, but the ceiling is going lower, and promises to go yet lower and lower, as is the case at the present time with the price of beef.
I am not pleading the cause of the individual farmer who, as probably some have done, put $5,000 into a number of feeder cattle and is now likely to take a real trimming, and

m robably is in a difficult financial position n ith the bank. I say I am not pleading for * idividual cases of this kind, although I know if1 ome who are going to lose half the money they jl iwn, because the farmer to a certain extent a s a gambler. He is a gambler on the weather, if he buys five or six carloads of cattle, and has some pasture to put them on, he hopes that the selling price of his commodity will be more than the price he pays for it. But I am pleading for consideration by the government of the effect on our whole war effort, in respect of our production capacity; because when you fix a ceiling price on beef, and then lower it a cent in July, another cent in August, and a cent and a half in September, someone might figure out for me how a man who bought stocker cattle in March and April and May is going to make any money when he has to sell them in the fall.
I do not know who is advising the government. I know that the wartime prices and trade board, having fixed a ceiling, is reducing it month by month, making it possible for the government to place a ceiling and invite the packers to place the floor. There is no floor placed by the government on the price the farmer will take. I understand that the government contract price for beef to the government has been about 214 cents, but we were warned that after July 13 it will not be more than 191 cents dressed; then it will be reduced to 18J cents; then to 17i cents; then to 161 cents. I know it has been said by no less an authority than the Minister of Finance that there is no fixed price on cattle; there is only a fixed price on beef. But the situation is more ridiculous than that. The government fixes a ceiling for the beef and the packer fixes a floor for the cattle, and there is no reason why he has to pay more than 7 cents, if he can buy them. When they are butchered eventually they will be sold I assume, at 3i cents less than 194.
Why say 7 cents when he did pay 13?

Because you have done nothing to prevent him from paying 7 cents if he can buy them at 7 cents. You have made it impossible for him to pay 13 cents, and you have so ordered things now that he must reduce the price to the farmer at least a couple of cents, and if he wants to reduce it more he can do so.
I say again that I am not pleading that the farmer should make more money. I am not even urging in this? instance equality of sacrifice, though I think it would be a fair plea to make. I realize that the situation is grave. I realize what the government are endeavouring to do, but I do not agree with

The Budget-Mr. Rowe
the methods they are employing. I say that they are unfair to the farmer and equally prejudicial to the war effort of this dominion, because no person can tell me-dozens have already told me the reverse-that this will improve agricultural production.
On what basis would the hon. member set a floor on the price of cattle? '
I would say it was just as fair to set a floor on what the farmer has to sell as to set a ceiling on what the packer has to buy.

How would you place
a ceiling on beef?

The ceiling is now set, and the floor could be set as well. It will simply mean that, as regards the man who bought his cattle last spring, he will not buy any next spring, and he will sell cattle that are half-fattened now and take a loss of one cent a pound rather than endure a loss of two and a half cents or more. There will be thousands of pounds of beef that would otherwise have been produced this summer that will not be produced. I am not pleading for a reckless rise in prices. It is true we had a rise in prices in the last great war; but I am wondering, from the point of view of the war effort, whether the setting of a ceiling will help our war production when there will be thousands of starving people in Europe, when our troops will be wanting foodstuffs, and when our own people are doing without beef now in certain parts of the country. Imagine the pass we have come to when our own people are looking for beef and cannot buy it. That is the climax to the lopsided development of agriculture which we have had in this country for a number of years, and now we have this fantastic method that will definitely result in lower production. The people will be discouraged, and why not? The farmers are faced with a great many uncertainties at any time, but this uncertainty is the greatest with which any industry has had to cope. There is not an industry in Canada that has been told, "Your product will go down a cent a pound one month, a cent a pound the next month, and will keep on going down until next winter". High prices were maintained when the farmer was buying; low prices are imposed when he has to sell. The government should give careful consideration to these novel methods in connection with its agricultural policy, instead of looking for advice from men who are not practically engaged in agriculture.
We have eight boards, We have a book full of them. There is not one single practical farmer on any one of these boards;
that is, any farmer who is actually dependent upon agriculture for his living. I am urging upon the government a policy that will meet this situation squarely, because we might as well face the facts, and the outstanding fact is that we are likely to be in this war for a long time. There are thousands of acres of land now lying idle in my own county and thousands lying idle in counties all around. There will be thousands of cattle turned on the market unless the government establishes a floor. The floor will be placed by the buyer at a point away lower than farmer's cost. What is being done now will put a damper on cattle feeding right across the dominion, and not only as regards grass-fed cattle. There will be fewer cattle fed next winter. The same principle applies all the way down the line.
I realize that the purpose is to avoid inflation. Someone will say that we must not allow runaway prices to control our commodities, because that will be the beginning of inflation. Again I urge the government to reconsider the whole matter and to take stock of the farmer's position. His farm was mortgaged when the war began, and he is now paying double and, in some instances, three times the price for his help which he was paying at that time. I know one farmer who is paying $1,000 to his man besides providing a house, a cow and a garden. He knows this is a high price; he knows it is two and a half times what he paid the man before, but he had no alternative except closing his gate. He says, "I cannot make money, but with my boys overseas I feel that I owe it to my country to keep the farm functioning and I cannot do it myself".
Members of this house are receiving letters from men working from four o'clock in the morning until twelve at night, struggling with large dairy herds, ploughing hard and difficult summerfallows, and still they are behind. Indeed, many of them will be unable to get their wheat in because of a shortage of labour. If these men want to continue operating, they have to pay wages commensurate with the competitive prices offered by industry. I have made the statement before, and I repeat it now, that even with the high prices that farmers are now paying for labour, they are not as high as industry can and does pay under present union wage scales. There is not, with present prices, a single farm commodity that would give the farmer a higher return than would represent a reasonable profit on his investment, maintaining the wage scale he has to pay in competition with the market, interest on his investment and a reasonable wage for himself and his wife.
The Budget-Mr. Rowe

The reason for this novel type of policy is that we have not one practical farmer representing agriculture on any of the boards we have in Canada, either agriculture or any other. I maintain that the industry which we have talked about as the backbone of the dominion, the industry that is now depended upon to produce commodities that are, we are told, as important to the country as shells and guns, should be better represented. Hon. gentlemen told the farmers in their campaign of the importance of agriculture to the dominion and urged them to keep on producing. Well, if the farmer belongs to such an important class of citizens, it is passing strange that we cannot find among the hundreds of thousands of them one farmer who is fit, if not to represent some other important branch of our natural resources, at least his own industry. The steel producers have representatives on boards; the pulpwood people have their representatives; the timber men have their representatives, and so have the merchandisers, the drygoods men and the Canada Packers. It is high time that the farmer in Canada got a square deal, and a square deal not only in a period of crisis but normally.
Is not Mr. Taggart a representative of agriculture?
He is an ex-minister of agriculture, but he is not dependent on farming for his living-no more dependent upon it than the present Minister of Agriculture of Canada.
He operates a big farm, though.
Yes, but he has not been close to farmer problems in the last many years, as other men have been who have been dependent upon farming and upon farming alone.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are many farmers
on advisory committees. I will get a list of them.

Yes. I have a list of them, but they are not trusted on the main committee. ^ They are on advisory committees, and their advice is not listened to. I could point to a thousand who are on advisory committees; you will meet them in the country later. The farmers are up in arms because of the novel policies that are carried out by men who are merely theorists without practical experience.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No representative of any
industry is on the wartime prices and trade board. They are all civil servants. They are not representing any industry.
What about your dollar-ayear men? I have no objection to the dollar-a-year men. There are some excellent men-

You should
have objection to dollar-a-year men.

My hon. friend perhaps has had
some experience with some of them which I have not had; but I believe, despite what the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lacroix) says, that there are some able men who are giving their service to the country. Perhaps there are some who are not as good as might be desired. But I do not believe that these boards are any better off, so far as agriculture is concerned, for having civil servants on them. I do not know that a civil servant who has been receiving from $6,000 to $8,000 a year, while farmers have had mortgages on their farms in the last ten years, is as well qualified to meet the problem of production at the present time, as the man who is going through the sweat and toil of actual experience, without help, and who has had to put up with these difficult years. From the point of view of our war production it is high time the government listened to the men who know what it costs to produce a bushel of wheat or a pound of butter rather than say haphazardly when beef goes a little high, "we will put a price on it." Butter is now fixed at 35 cents a pound-
It is not fixed at that; that is the ceiling.
Yes, and it can go as low as it likes.
There is a floor under it too.
Now the minister is going to bonus it.
No, I am not going to bonus it.
He was against bonuses in 1935.

There is a war on now.
I was against a lot of things.
The minister had a political war on then.
My political wars have been about as successful as yours.
Probably more so.

I do not intend to pursue the issue further. I warn the government, if they do not want the most important branch of our production to go down in

The Budget-Mr. Rowe
dismal failure, to beware of fixing prices, while the farmer has rising costs which, by the very nature of the industry, the government cannot fix. I am not asking the government to fix the hired man's wages when he can get more money at the factory, but while the farmer has that uncertainty, do not impose on him another uncertainty which will cripple his ability to produce what is so essential to victory and equally important in peace.
The minister has a difficult task. Probably the most painful thing a minister has to do is to impose more taxes. I realize that the government must give some consideration with regard to taxing enterprises to the limit of what they can stand, or even "killing the goose that lays the golden egg". I am alarmed at the amount that is being spent for ordinary services, despite the war requirements. It is necessary that the nation be assured that the money is spent honestly. I am not charging that it is not, but the next thing to dishonest spending is reckless and extravagant spending for civilian purposes and services that we could do without at this time.
I give this suggestion to the minister in all sincerity as a solution of the problem of avoiding diminishing returns, namely that in the taxation of industry there might be some exemption made for post-war rehabilitation, research and so forth, so that they can be ready to give employment to the thousands of returned men after the war. Such action would go a long way to warn enabling industry to equip itself to compete in post-war markets and provide openings for our returned men, many of whom will be skilled mechanics.
I compliment the minister upon the compulsory savings feature. I mentioned it in the house some time ago. He did not think as much of it when I mentioned it as I did when he put it into effect. But I give the minister a further suggestion. I urge him to give further consideration to the exemption of life insurance premiums. I compliment him upon exempting the premiums of those who are of more mature years, but I urge and plead that he give consideration to the young men getting married now. In these days of uncertainty, surely if you, Mr. Speaker, and I are entitled to exemption, what about the boy who has not a home to live in, who cannot find one even if he could afford to pay for it, especially in Ottawa, and who takes to himself a wife? He has to pay all the income tax we have to pay and, if he wants to put 83,000 on his life in order to give his wife a little security, he does
not get the same privilege as those who have carried insurance for years. I do not think we should be exempted if the same privilege is not extended to him. I think upon further consideration the minister will include that.
I realize that he might be afraid of people taking out large policies, but that could be overcome by regulation, limiting the amount or limiting it to men of a certain age.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman think there would be any objection on the score that the government would be giving a tremendous impetus to the life insurance business by such a measure as he suggests?
That is not the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be the result.

I understand the minister perhaps being alarmed or feeling that he was doing almost a favour to the life insurance companies. But what sounder way is there for a man to save? What better security and what better provision can a man make in case anything should happen to him? Succession duties bring most of it back to the treasury anyway. It makes a liquid asset when a man dies, so that the estate does not have to sacrifice assets on account of market fluctuations, and I believe that any slight advantage it gives to the life insurance companies is not hurtful because if we strengthen the insurance companies of this dominion, we strengthen the economic and financial fabric of the dominion.
I am not speaking for any insurance company;
I have paid them more than they have paid me so far, fortunately. But if the government is going to restrict rigidly the income of individuals by taxation, it should go a long way also to encourage thrift among our people, and I do not know any way that it can better encourage thrift than by that process.
I also urge the minister to consider exempting, to the extent of the compulsory saving tax, war savings certificates that may be purchased during the year. I have had some experience with the sale of war savings certificates, and I know the minister knows, without admitting it, that thousands upon thousands of war savings certificate holders are selling them rapidly at the present time.
Is that true?
Yes, and they are going to sell them. I do not criticize the minister for not including it-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member does not mean selling them?
The Budget-Mr. Rowe
Yes, selling them; thousands are selling them and refusing to buy more.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are not transferable.
The hon. member means cashing them in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Redeeming them.

They have to cash them in. I urge the minister to give consideration to exempting war savings certificates. I think the result would be almost the same to the treasury. Deduction could be made at the source as now, thus avoiding a tremendous amount of additional detail work. The compulsory savings are repayable two years after the cessation of hostilities, whereas war savings certificates are redeemable after seven and a half years. The adoption of this suggestion would encourage people to buy even beyond the amount they now buy, and leave it as a Voluntary operation.
I leave that thought with the minister. He may have the matter well in hand, but I would also suggest that in maintaining a balanced economy it is essential that every effort be made to place new bond issues outside the banks. In the first place it is an essential check on inflation, and in the second place the responsibility now on the banks is tremendous and will become greater as the war progresses. To meet this requirement, consideration should be given to issuing, in the future, securities that will be more attractive to non-banking lenders and less attractive to banks. I think that could be arranged. The minister might also give consideration to issuing registered bonds, nonnegotiable for a period of time, to which commercial banks would be forbidden to subscribe or to hold for a stated period. These bonds could be kept on sale continuously, like war savings certificates, and subscriptions applied for could be fully allotted at all times. I am not going to enlarge on these suggestions; I'had not intended to speak at this length. I believe, however, that an issue of this kind would check further expansion of bank deposits and would be particularly attractive to insurance companies and other investors outside the banks. I believe borrowing from bank credits as an alternative comes close to outright inflation, and as such is a hazardous course to follow unless it is considered absolutely necessary. Borrowing from the banks does not reflect itself in direct sacrifices by the people, with the result that huge expenditures are made without an actual realization by the people of the seriousness of the situation.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that I am not at all discouraged or pessimistic

about this country being able to meet the obligations placed upon it by the minister. We are going to win this war. Our national determination, together with our great resources, will enable us to carry forward our war^ effort if only we have full equality of sacrifice and opportunity for service. In that regard I again urge the government to be careful to see that the agricultural producers of this country are given a square deal, not only in fairness to these people themselves, but for the more important consideration of the victory that is ahead.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank you for the decision you rendered a short time ago, ruling that I should be allowed to speak at this time. I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) upon his presentation of the budget. One can well imagine the tremendous amount of work that had to be performed in carrying out his thankless task, which is to provide the money required by the government.
It is not my intention to undertake a survey of the budget. In that regard I feel as a man might who had reached the foot of the highest mountain in the Rockies. He would not feel like trying to put that mountain on his shoulders, to carry it to some place where the surface was more level. This matter is too important for me to try to cover everything, but I should like to add a few remarks to what has been said by those who have already spoken. I think the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) made an admirable speech, in which he brought out some of the weak points of this taxation scheme. In the course of his remarks he touched upon the income tax as it affects married people with children, and dealt with its effect upon those with more than three dependents. I shall not repeat all his arguments, Mr. Speaker, since I understand it is your desire that we should not speak at great length, but anyone looking over the speech of the hon. gentleman can see how he dealt with these measures of taxation. He had this to say, as reported at page 3793 of Hansard, with regard to large families:
People cannot afford to have children. If Canada is to be a great nation in the future she must have greater population, and the most satisfactory wav to achieve an increase in population is to encourage the raising of children steeped in Canadian tradition rather than through immigration of persons steeped in the traditions of other lands.
Surely that is a good principle. Moreover,
I should like to point out that it is from these large families, which are ordinarily found in Quebec, where they have ten, twelve and fifteen children, we find as many as five or six brothers in the army. I could name, offhand, several

The Budget-Mr. Roy
families who have contributed several sons: the Guertins, the Lemieuxs, the Chenels, the Fourniers, the Reeders, the Pattersons and the Keaneys. So we realize the importance to the nation of large families such as these; and I do not think there is any fairness in taxing the father of ten or twelve children to within a few hundred dollars of the amount we tax a single man. I believe the government should look into this taxation scheme and see if greater fairness could not be achieved in connection with those of our people who are heads of large families, and who constitute more than one-half of our population, and the most important capital of a nation.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was about to make a few comments on the speeches of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore). However, since I have agreed with the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Raymond) to .be as short as possible, I shall defer my remarks for the time being. Those speeches were truly Canadian and should prove an inspiration to the population of Canada. I should like to refer also to the speeches made yesterday, the 75th anniversary of confederation, by the leaders of the different groups. I think those speeches should also prove an inspiration to the whole of Canada and I hope they will do some good. I had intended to make a few remarks about the inequalities of the sugar rationing system, but I may have an opportunity to make them on the resolution stage. The importance of the budget has been stressed by the leader of the opposition pretty well in this phrase. The leader of the opposition generally speaks quite well when he gets away from the conscription of men for overseas. He said this, as reported at page 3789 of Hansard:
Just imagine a total budget expenditure of almost four billions of dollars for this little nation of less than twelve million souls-more than $333 for every man, woman and child in Canada! What a task to raise by various means, this vast sum of money!
This matter has been so well stressed that it does not call for any comment from me. I wonder if there is going to be anything left out of these vast sums to provide for the equipment and the defence of our two coasts which are threatened by invasion? Half of it is destined for England, and a considerable
proportion of the rest is to be used to equip, maintain and increase our armed forces overseas with volunteers and conscripts as well. There will not remain much for the defence of Canada, and to take care of the most imperious need in our national economy. I shall probably have further opportunity to discuss the defence of Canada on the committee stage of Bill No. 80.
I should like to say a few words in connection with the important problem of supplying oil for our own needs and the needs of our allies. I refer hon. members to the speech made yesterday by the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene). He demonstrated our need for oil and the importance of the government discovering new sources. Although I have great esteem for the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe); I appreciate the great task he is doing, but I do not agree with him when he answered, as he did on June 8, a question put by me and also one put by the leader of the Social Credit group about the necessity of securing some oil. His answer was that the government had no tools or would not be doing any drilling to discover oil.
There is no reason why the government should not make an effort to discover new sources of oil. The supply of oil will have a bearing upon the survival of the allies. I think everyone will admit that oil is the most important factor in victory. The government had no tools to build ships and tanks or to make guns and many other articles, but government companies were formed and the same thing could be done here. It would appear that the allies are about to lose their last sources of oil in Iraq and Iran, so it is about time that something should be done. In 1941 Mr. Cottrelle, the oil controller, is reported by the newspapers to have said that there would not be one cent of government money spent in prospecting for oil as long as he was in that position. Where does that gentleman get his authority to control this house and the government? I do not think we should listen to him. We should take immediate steps to provide new sources of oil. For this reason, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe):
That all the words after the word "that" in the motion be ueleted and the following words substituted therefor:
"It is expedient that proper measures be taken in order to secure new sources of oil from all possibilities offered by petroleum areas that Canada may have."
Mr. MAXIME RAYMOND (Beauharnois-
Laprairie) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty) recalled last

The Budget-Mr. Raymond

Monday that the figures quoted by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the ministers of the various defence departments and the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), established that our country, taking into account the size of its population, was furnishing a greater effort in this war than any other of the united nations. That is a statement we should do well to ponder when the Canadian people are being asked to make new sacrifices totally out of proportion with their means. Indeed the new budget calls for such an increase in taxation that a large number of families will be unable to meet their obligations; and if we compare it to the budgets of other allied countries, we must conclude that our war effort is increasing in a much greater degree than any other.
I demonstrated to the house last year, not without scandalizing a certain few, that the fiscal demands made on the Canadian taxpayer by the war were greater than those made on the English taxpayer. At the risk of scandalizing the same few, I now intend to show that the present budget further augments the Canadian taxpayer's burden to an extent not yet reached by the English taxpayer.
The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Ferland) quoted certain figures showing that the single man is more heavily burdened in England than in this country, but to arrive at such a conclusion he had to deduct from the Canadian tax the amount representing the minimum savings requirement, a deduction he omitted in the case of the English tax. The parallel he drew is thus fundamentally wrong and proves nothing. The figures I shall quote include those released by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Sir Kingsley Wood, in his budget address of April 14 last and in the accompanying white book, as well as those furnished to the house by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) on June 23.
In order to determine the extent of the fiscal demands made upon us by the war both in England and in Canada, let us first examine the situation that obtained in the fiscal year which preceded the conflict, noting the sum total of the taxes levied in both countries in the year 1938-39 and comparing them with those of the following periods. Mr. Speaker, we meet to-night in the greatest crisis that has visited this empire at any time in our history. We are discussing the largest budget which has ever been presented to a Canadian parliament, in order to ensure that Canada's contribution shall be all that it should be in the battle for the survival of freedom.
It is a tremendous budget. I congratulate the minister upon the courage he has shown in introducing this budget, bringing home to the Canadian people the awfulness of the prospect before us unless victory is ours. I congratulate, too, the Canadian people upon the reception they have given to this budget which will mean so much to them.
But this evening I am not going to discuss or to make any recommendations or suggestions in connection with the budget as such. That I shall reserve until the matter comes into the resolution stage. I intend to discuss a trend which is gradually becoming more pronounced as the war goes on and is against the full operation of our parliamentary institutions and all that they stand for in the democratic way of life.
Parliament, has a serious responsibility. This parliament represents the people of Canada; it is the repository and trustee of their hopes of survival. Economic freedom is very important, but important, too, is the matter of our political and personal freedoms, and these things must not be lost sight of during these trying days of war. I have no apologies to offer for speaking on this subject; for this is the only place, the only forum, where one can express one's views, where one can make one's criticisms, where one can advance constructively such ideas as one believes are in the interests of the country as a whole.
To-day, in the British House of Commons, the Prime Minister of Great Britain, referring to the debate which has gone on there during the past two days, said that he was "in favour of freedom of expression" in the commons, and he pointed out that "no other country would use or dare to use such freedom in times of mortal peril" such as those through which we are passing. We hear too often that parliament is not living up to its responsibilities, and I think that we who enjoy the privilege and responsibility of being members have the right to place before the country our views in regard to the necessity of the retention of those rights-rights for which this empire fights-so long as thereby the war effort is not impeded. I believe it will be agreed by all hon. members that the progress of Canada's war effort has been in

large measure due to criticism offered in this house and by the press, resulting in the formation of public opinion.
Churchill to-day received an overwhelming vote of confidence in the British House of Commons. He has always appreciated and welcomed criticism and has often stated that one of the salient differences between the axis nations and countries belonging to the united nations is that the former fear and the latter invite criticism. Parliament is being criticized in the press and throughout the country for failing to appreciate the responsibility which rests upon it. I think in this parliament we have the right to the expression of our ideals, our conceptions of those freedoms for which we fight, so long as we do not thereby impair the war effort or give benefit to the enemy.
To-day the government exercises a greater control over parliament than ever before in the history of this country. It exercises a greater control over the freedom of expression of the press and public men throughout Canada than ever before. But if there is one thing which we as members must demand, it is that criticism shall continue, that criticism shall not be curtailed so long as it is designed to spur on the government to greater effort; and we have the right to demand that in so far as conditions permit, legislation passed in respect of matters particularly domestic shall be passed by parliament and not through the instrumentality of orders in council.
There is a tendency on the part of this government not to give the attention to parliament that it should, and we are approaching a state where parliament need not be called together except for the purpose of voting supply.
In support of my statement that there is a trend away from true parliamentary government, I refer once more, what I have referred to at other times, to the attitude of the government in continuing in ever-increasing measure to govern by order in council, with the result that we in this parliament are denied the opportunity of debate on matters which affect the welfare of the people as a whole.
As an example of this trend, the wartime prices and trade regulations which were introduced by order in council while parliament was sitting. Many difficulties have arisen in connection with the administration of these regulations, all because of the fact that parliament was and is denied the opportunity of debating them. Only to-day the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) drew

The Budget-Mr. Diejenbaker
attention to the effect of arbitrary regulations passed by boards and commissions on the agricultural industry. When one considers that while parliament is in session, orders in council are being passed with ever-accelerated regularity, I think the time has come when we as members of parliament should ask the government to give more consideration to parliament in the passing of legislation.
There is not a lawyer who is able to advise a client as to what the law is in reference to any statute in Canada without looking into the matter of orders in council. When only the other day I asked a question of one of the departments of government as to what orders in council had been passed that affect the statutes under its jurisdiction, the answer was that many of them had been placed in the Canada Gazette, which implies that many have not received publicity in that publication.
Further, as indicating the trend, I would point out that we as members are gradually having our rights curtailed through the denial to us of private members day. I realize the need for action and for immediate action in many matters. I do think, however, that if the rules of parliament which permit forty-minute speeches are found difficult of operation during war time, then there should be a revision of the rules; but the right of private members day should not be denied, and it should be recalled that it was not denied in the last war except, in part, until the last six months.
The denial of the right of those who do not belong to the government to utilize the radio of this country in order to place their points of view before the country is another matter. It is true the situation in this regard may not be as serious to-day as it was a few months ago, but the withdrawal of that restriction came about only in consequence of criticism in parliament. The government, when asked questions, many of which by no stretch of the imagination can be interpreted as being contrary to the public interest, in increasing measure relies upon the excuse that it is not in the public interest to reveal information.' What does that mean? It means that the government can deny members of parliament information upon the basis of which criticism might be levelled against the administration as a whole.
Then there is the further attitude, displayed more particularly recently by the government, of being allergic to fair and constructive criticism. It has seen fit to prosecute various newspapers in Canada under the defence of Canada regulations, and the reason has been the fact that these newspapers have been
criticizing the government in a manner that did not appeal to it. In connection with the investigation into the Hong Kong expedition the attitude of the government in refusing to table the evidence has resulted in preventing discussion in 'parliament, thereby preventing criticism based on the facts as revealed- by the evidence, although I do realize that in time of war it is necessary to exercise discretion and not to permit the publication of evidence that might in any way injure the war effort of the country or be of benefit to the enemy. The position of the Canadian people so far as that report is concerned is that they are denied the opportunity of seeing all pertinent parts of the evidence, while they are permitted to see a part of the evidence that bears out the decision of the commissioner in charge.
A further example might be mentioned in passing. There has been a change in this respect since the present Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) took office. It is that of men who were interned after having their cases brought before committees set up by the minister, and although no wrong doing was established against them, yet in certain cases the minister refused to carry out the recommendations of the committee. On the other hand in Great Britain, Sir Norman Birkett has stated that the practice is that no man has been interned or proceeded against for merely criticizing the government, for words spoken, but that such proceedings are taken only for overt acts. I realize that in war time censorship is necessary; criticism should not be made which might in any way impair the war effort. That is why the defence of Canada regulations were passed by order in council under the powers contained in the War Measures Act. Those regulations were intended to cover dangerous men and their activities and to permit the government to act quickly without having to have recourse to the ordinary channels of the criminal law. Under the criminal code there is provision for the prosecution of men who endeavour to undermine the country in time of war. There is provision to deal with treasonable offences, and with sedition, which require proof on the part of the prosecution of circumstances from which the wrongful intent of the accused may be deduced. The defence of Canada regulations give to the government of the day, through the Minister of Justice, the power to proceed by way of action against men, however honest their purpose, however patriotic their desires, who say anything that the government does not consider in the public interest; and the only defence they have is the right to prove to the satisfaction of the court that what they have said was said in good faith and merely to
The Budget-Mr. Diejenbaker

criticize or to point out errors or defects in the conduct of the government. I now draw attention to the two pertinent sections in our regulations and compare them with the corresponding sections in England. Section 39A reads:
No person shall-
(a)	act in any manner, spread reports, or make statements or utterances intended or likely to cause disaffection to His Majesty or to interfere with the success of His Majesty's forces or of the forces of any allied or associated powers or to prejudice His Majesty's relations with foreign powers.
(b)	act in any manner, spread reports, or make statements or utterances intended or likely to prejudice the recruiting, training, discipline, or administration of any of His Majesty's forces;
The question of intent does not enter into the matter at all. The mere making of a statement or a criticism, however honest and honourable it may be, permits of the prosecution of the man who makes such statement or criticism. By reason of the fact that it is an extraordinary power to deny to the accused the right to be proceeded against under the criminal code, there is a prerequisite which the prosecution must be able to establish. I quote:
A prosecution for an offence against regulations 39, 39A or 39C of these regulations shall not be instituted except by, or with the consent of, counsel representing the Atorney-General of Canada or of the province: Provided that this paragraph shall not prevent the arrest or the issue, or the execution of a warrant for the arrest, of any person in respect of any such offence, or the remanding, in custody or on bail, of any person charged with such offence.
In other words, the position is this, that any man in this dominion to-day, any man in this parliament, any loyal citizen of this country, can be proceeded against, brought before a court of law and found guilty if the statements that he made are "intended to or likely to" have resulted in a diminution of recruiting. There is not a member of this house or a member of a legislature anywhere in this dominion who voices, inside or outside this house, a criticism, the effect of which might be likely to interfere with recruiting, who might not be convicted under these regulations. It does not require any intent.
Let me call attention to a judgment based on a similar section of the regulations. The reason why I do this is to say to the government that they should never use these regulations unless there is no other means open to them, unless to proceed by way of indictment under the criminal code is not available because of the dangerous nature of the acts committed by the accused. In a judgment of the court of appeal of Ontario in Rex v. Stewart in 1940, a judgment of the chief justice of Ontario concurred in by the other judges,

the judgment indicates that a man with an honest motive, a desire to help, a wish to contribute to the war effort, would be guilty of an offence under this section even though he had no intent or guilty mind, and the chief justice of Ontario said:
(The regulations) were made in the emergency of war then threatened and now in progress. They prohibit, in terms that are absolute, certain acts that may interfere with or prejudice the preparations and efforts made for the successful carrying on of the war, or that may be prejudicial to the safety of the state. It would seem plain that both the subject matter and the purpose of the regulations, as well as the terms in which they are expressed make it necessary to hold that their prohibitions are absolute, and that it is not a defence in a prosecution for their breach to say that what was done was done in ignorance or without intending any harm. The acts prohibited are to be stopped.
That judgment shows that if the Minister of Justice of Canada in his .capacity as Attorney General, or the attorney general of a province, looks into the matter and decides, by reason of what a certain man has said, that he is dangerous, this particular section, far, from being a protection in time of war, can become an instrument of tyranny against those with whom the government disagrees.
They have no such provisions in England. The provisions there are that:
No person shall-(a) endeavour by means of any false statement, false document or false report to influence public opinion ... in a manner likely to be prejudicial to the defence of the realm or the efficient prosecution of the war.
In other words, in England there must be an intent, in that there must be falsity in the statement made by the person accused.
I wonder how many hon. members realize that under the defence of Canada regulations to-day a man might make a statement that was absolutely true and yet be guilty of an offence if in the estimation of the attorney general of the dominion or an attorney general of a province he should be prosecuted if the statement made was "intended to or likely to" impede the war effort. I think the time has come when we as members of parliament should protest against the use of these sections for the prosecution of persons other than those who seek to- undermine the government of the state or the war effort. However high-minded and patriotic the accused or his purpose, he is guilty if certain results flow therefrom or are "likely to".
These are extraordinary sections. They were never intended to be used for the prosecution of political opponents. Their use should be circumscribed within the limits of the section itself. There is not a member of this house, there is not an honourable,

The Budget-Mr. Isnor
patriotic citizen anywhere in Canada who may not be convicted of an offence under these sections if they are used against him and provided the Minister of Justice sees fit to consent to proceedings being taken against him. I say the time has come for hon. members to stand up for their rights and the rights of loyal citizens all over this dominion, and to secure from the government the assurance that these sections will no longer be used against loyal fcitizens of proven patriotism. If we do not do that, the day of freedom of political speech and the independence of patriotic citizens and newspapers throughout Canada in voicing fair criticism in order to improve conditions and to spur on the war effort of this dominion is past. I think we as a parliament should take a decided stand that we will not give approval to possible future political prosecutions, and that stand must be taken now. These sections are necessary in order to assure that our war effort shall not be undermined'; but as members of [DOT] parliament, irrespective of party, it becomes our duty to tell the government now and finally that we will not tolerate their use in order to proceed against members of this house or honourable citizens outside the house whose purposes in making criticism are high-minded and patriotic.
I make no suggestion that these sections are being so used, but I do point out the danger of their being used against political opponents in time of war. I suggest that even the appearance of the government playing politics in matters such as this is dangerous to the unity of the war effort and will of the Canadian people. I further say that political prosecutions-or persecutions if you will-whether of members of parliament or of public men are dangerous to public morale when the public, or a large portion of the public, believe, whether rightly or wrongly, they are being used for that purpose. This is the only place where these things can be asserted; and as members of parliament irrespective of party we should take our stand and say to the government, "So far you may go in the interests of the safety of the state, but in proceeding against citizens of proven honour, patriotism and integrity, if an offence has allegedly been committed, the proceedings should be under the criminal code". Surely parliament is not to be denied the right; surely members of parliament are not to be denied the right, to criticize the possible use of these sections for improper purposes. A government that indicts an honest, patriotic citizen under these sections indicts itself as being fearful of criticism. I ask hon. members in all parts of this house to take
the attitude that has been taken in England since the beginning of the war and now, so well epitomized in the words of the Prime Minister of Great Britain, speaking in the House of Commons on January 22, 1941, when he used these words:
His Majesty's government welcome all the impulse which the House of Commons and press and public opinion of this island can give to us in driving forward our war effort and trying to gain an earlier inch or a more fruitful hour wherever it may be possible. But I have no doubt that the house, in its overwhelming majority, will wish to give its tribute of encouragement, as well as its dose of correction, and will lend its own heave of loyal strength to the forward surges that now have begun.
We meet here in difficult and trying times. If ever there was a time when we should be united in a common purpose, that time is now. If ever there was a time when the provisions of these sections should not be invoked against citizens who are known for their loyalty and devotion to their country, it is now and in the tiying weeks that are to come. I have pointed out the trend. I think as members of parliament we have a right to insist that the trend away from true democratic principles shall end, except where the public interest and the safety of the state demand a departure therefrom.
Mr. GORDON B. ISNOR (Halifax): Mr. Speaker, I fully realize the awkward position in which I find myself, having to follow such a brilliant speaker with the legal training of the hon. member (Mr. Diefenbaker) who has just resumed his seat. I do not propose to try to follow his reasoning; I am going to stay as closely as a business man can to the subject before the house and deal with the budget, and only the budget.
As a background to what I have to say may I give a little of my own history. From 1928 to 1935 I was a member of the Nova Scotia legislature. For five years I sat in the opposition there, facing, among others, the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) who now sits in this house as a member of the opposition. In 1935 I resigned my seat to become a candidate in the federal general election, and have been here since that time endeavouring to represent the constituency of Halifax, along with my colleague from that city. I well recall that during those seven or eight years, as a business man I was interested in financial matters, and particularly in the budget; and during the whole time I was in the legislature, both as a member of the opposition and while sitting on the government side, I took an active part in the budget debates. They were quite
The Budget-Mr. Isnor

different there from those that are carried on here to-day. As the hon. member for Cumberland will remember, it was a matter of the opposition criticizing the government in power over the amount of the funded debt; pointing out the extravagant expenditures, as all opposition members do, and so on. At the same time I believe I did offer some constructive suggestions, and I believe the government of the day appreciated that fact. I am sure the hon. member for Cumberland would say that in my remarks I always endeavoured to be fair.

The credit regulations whereby purchases made in one month had to be paid for the next month were also beneficial both for the store and its customers. All these regulations have, I believe, made it possible for the businessman or storekeeper to carry on and meet his obligations under this budget.
I was rather surprised at the criticism made by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party (Mr. Coldweil) and by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) in regard to the effects of the change in exemptions for dependents. I shall only touch upon that briefly because the Minister of Finance will deal with it much more fully and clearly than I can; but from what .study I have been able to give it, the wage-earner in the $2,500 income bracket, a married man with one or two children, is in a much better position under the new exemption provisions than he was under the old. Under the old provisions he had an exemption of $400 for each child, which at 15 per cent meant an exemption of $60. That is $20 less than under the present arrangement, which allows a deduction of $80 for each child, and I am not taking into consideration the deduction under the normal or national defence tax which may also be coming to him.
I wish to congratulate either the Minister of Finance or his advisers or the government -it really does not matter to whom the credit is due so long as the plan is a good one and brings the desired results-upon introducing the compulsory savings feature in connection with the income tax. I believe it is an extremely fine plan which will be helpful to both the businessman and the average wage-earner, and I congratulate the minister upon introducing this provision in his comprehensive plan of budgeting.
There was a doubt, I think, in the minds of one or two speakers as to the effect which this compulsory saving might have on savings bank deposits and the purchase of war savings stamps and war savings certificates. Naturally the compulsory saving will be reflected somewhat in these other directions; but whatever effect it might have had upon bank deposits and the purchase of war savings stamps and certificates a year ago, I believe that the benefits to-day will more than outweigh any disadvantages.
I want to say a word about tax deductions at the source. I have had experience in 
dealing with deductions in connection with the national defence tax, and I have also had to make deductions from the pay of employees for the purchase of war savings stamps. This tax deduction feature has, I believe, been welcomed by all classes of our people who have to pay taxes. It is just one more step in the direction of facilitating and systematizing the collection and payment of taxes. Only a few days ago I noticed in the press that a survey had been made and a large number of persons interviewed and asked ' their opinion with regard to this question:	Would you prefer having your
income tax deducted regularly from income at the source? As I looked over the long list of those interviewed, I found that without exception everyone favoured such a plan or scheme. I was particularly impressed with the interview granted by J. W. Berry, general manager of the Guaranty Trust Company of Toronto. Mr. Berry said:
I would prefer to have my income tax deducted regularly at the source. Personnally, I recognize the necessity of providing for income taxes and would welcome an orderly progressive discharge of this obligation.
He goes on:
From the national viewpoint, I think income tax deduction at the source equally preferable in that such a plan would firstly, provide the government with a continuous flow of revenue to be used in its pay-as-you-go plan; secondly, would simplify collection methods and eliminate the possibility of arrears and loss. Thirdly, it would help curb purchasing power which is vitally necessary if living costs are to be controlled and income directed into those channels which provide the sinews of war.
That statement expresses my view in as concise and definite a manner as I could express it were I to spend a week in trying to compress it into a paragraph or two. Mr. Berry in this interview strikes at the root of this whole budget scheme when he remarks, "It would help curb purchasing power which is vitally necessary if living costs are to be controlled"; and that, I think, is a feature which the Minister of Finance had in mind when he introduced this budget plan.
Will this budget prove a success? I believe it will. I believe so for the reasons already outlined, namely, that general employment is up 22 per cent and employment in manufacturing is rip 30 per cent over last year.
I understand that general manufacturing employment has gone up something like 80 per cent since the beginning of the war. Retail sales as I have already indicated, went up 20 per cent last year, and since pre-war days have increased by something like 50 per cent.

All-over control by the government of prices and wages, as I have already mentioned, is the third feature of it.
I might mention another important factor which the Minister of Finance brought to our attention when he presented the budget, namely restrictions in connection with travel. He stated1-and I was astonished at the large amount-that in the two years in which the foreign exchange control board has operated, it has saved to the country something like 8100,000,000.

In times such as these, with heavy war expenditures, heavy taxes naturally follow. No one should complain about them if the money is to be used to win the war. Speaking of my own province, I think I can say we realize that there is a war on. From the very outbreak of war members of the various branches of the service were seen in numbers on our streets. We have watched them come by train and leave by ship for overseas. We see our ships entering and leaving the harbour. I believe that the people of Halifax, and of Nova Scotia in general, realize to a greater extent than other people just what this war means, and that is why I say I believe that in so far as Nova Scotians are concerned, the Minister of Finance need not worry about their taking their part in carrying the load and shouldering their portion of this budget.
I should like to mention my interest in social security. I do not know whether this is the time to do so. I had to face that question; I debated in Halifax whether this is an opportune time to bring in unemployment insurance. I think the main argument which convinced me that now is the time was the fact that there is a large amount of money in circulation, that wage-earners are earning steadily and in large amounts, and that, therefore, this is a good time to set up a reserve to take care of needs which may arise following the close of the war or if we should again be visited, which I hope we never shall, with another period of depression.
For the same reason I would suggest to the minister that he and his government give
serious consideration to the matter of old age pensions. I do not know whether I care to define at this time a particular age to which they should be lowered, but I believe it should be not more than sixty-five years, with a broadening of the provisions to take care of unemployables even at the age of sixty. Throughout the country there is a number of persons, suffering real hardship, who are unemployable. Not being returned soldiers, they do not receive any special consideration. I think that this class, though its numbers may not be great, should receive favourable consideration in this regard, and I hope the minister will take the matter into consideration for action at some future time.
May I also suggest that he should reconsider the amount paid. I believe that $20 a month is too low; and of course everybody does not receive $20; in Nova Scotia, I believe, the average is only $14.86 or $14.87. I think the minister should consider increasing the amount to $30. I know that the provinces, particularly those which have not now recourse to certain sources of revenue which they formerly could tap, may strenuously object to any such increase in so far as their contribution is concerned. For that reason I suggest that the federal government assume 85 per cent of the payment and that the provinces' share be reduced to the remaining 15 per cent. In other words, of a grant of $30, the federal government would contribute $25.50, and a province, $4.50, instead of $5 as at the present time.
I have one other suggestion to make, relating to retirements. In times like these, when young men, or men in certain age brackets, are required for active service and other duties of a strenuous nature, we should retain in the government employ those who are capable of carrying on their duties efficiently instead of permitting them to retire, as under the civil service regulations, at the age of sixty-five. I was particularly surprised the other evening to read in the paper that the Department of National Defence had retired a colonel at fifty-six years of age. I do not wish to give his name. I do not know the reason. I do not know the gentleman. But on general principles it struck me that this was not a time to retire men at the age of fifty-six. Surely the government could find some useful place in another department for any man of that age.
I commend the minister for the action he has taken in exempting all pensions of exservice men both of the last great war and of the present war. That is the proper thing to do and it has been well received. Several members who have already spoken have complimented the government in that regard. I
The Budget-Speaker's Ruling

suggest that he enlarge that a little to include all persons receiving pensions for total disabilities. I have particularly in mind the victims of the Halifax explosion, a large number of whom lost limbs-a leg, an arm, a hand or an eye. I do not think it is fair to tax such a person on the pension he or she receives. That is a special case which deserves special consideration.
I should like to have quoted, in closing, the last paragraph of the minister's speech, but time will not permit my doing so. However, I might call to the attention of the house the words of Mr. G. W. Spinney, chairman of the national war finance committee:
War is never cheap, but surely it is a thousand times cheaper to win than to lose.
If I have been at all convincing to those who have listened to me, whether in the opposition or in other parts of the house, I shall have done my duty if I have induced in them that frame of mind which will incline them, instead of being critical, to cooperate and to make known to the people of Canada the magnificent effort which the Minister of Finance has made in placing before the Canadian public a budget built along such comprehensive lines. I believe that with the cooperation of all it will be carried through to a successful issue. I am reminded of the words of J. Mason Knox:
It is not guns or armament Or the money they can pay,
It's the close cooperation That makes them win the day.
It is not the individual Or the army as a whole,
But the everlastin' teamwork of every bloomin' soul.

I have been considering the amendment moved by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy). The motion before
the house is:
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself again into committee of ways and means.
The amendment moved by the hon. member for Gaspe, seconded by the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe) is:
That all the words after the word "that" in the motion be deleted and the following words substituted therefor:
"It is expedient that proper measures be taken in order to secure new sources of oil from all possibilities offered by petroleum areas that Canada may have."
Standing order 48 provides:
When a question is under debate no motion is received unless to amend it; to postpone it to a day certain: for the previous question; for reading the orders of the day; for proceeding to another order; to adjourn the debate; or for the adjournment of the house.

Citation 395 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms reads:
It is an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed. Every amendment proposed to be made either to a question or to a proposed amendment should be so framed that if agreed to by the house the question or amendment as amended would be intelligible and consistent with itself.
If the house agrees to the amendment, it denies the right of the government to provide ways and means, or it postpones that period. The amendment is not relevant to the question before the house now, and -there is a further objection to its relevancy. In its form the amendment is a substantive motion. At page 420 Bourinot states:
The ordinary rules of debate are applicable on this occasion-
That is, with regard to an amendment on going into supply.
-for instance, a matter already decided by the house, or of which notice has been given, or which stands upon the orders of the day, cannot be discussed.
The same rule is stated in May, 13th edition, at pages 525-26, and in citation 398 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, which states:
An amendment cannot anticipate a notice of motion on the order paper.
I find on perusal of the order paper that, under "notices of motions", there is a motion standing in the name of the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene), which reads:
Whereas the largest known supply of gasoline and petroleum products in Canada, perhaps in the world, is procurable from the tar sands of the McMurray, Waterways and Fort McKay areas along the Athabaska and Clearwater rivers, in the constituency of Athabaska, Alberta, some three hundred and fifty miles from the city of Edmonton.
Therefore be it resolved,-That, in the opinion of this house, for the carrying on of our vital war effort, and supplying the needs of our farmers, manufacturers, transportation systems and tourist trade, the government should take into immediate consideration the advisability of assisting, by way of financing or otherwise, greatly increased production in this area of the gasoline and petroleum products so necessary to the people of Canada.
It is true the resolution, on the order paper refers to a particular area, but the discussion of that resolution would, of course, involve the discussion of other oil areas of Canada, and the house would be asked to act accordingly. For the reasons I have given, and on the authorities I have cited, I must rule the amendment out of order.

maintopic: COMPARATIVE STATEMENT OF INCOME TAX PAYABLE IN CANADA AND BRITAIN FOR THE YEAR 1942
speechtext:
The 1942-43 budget is only a new edition of

The Budget-Mr. Hlynka
another debt-creating and tax-draining document. The only difference between this budget and those which the government has brought down in the past is that this one is much largeT and heavier. It calls for greater expenditure than did the budgets which have preceded it, but in principle the present budget is framed identically along the same lines that all other budgets were, which were brought in by this government.
I must say that there are three good features about the present budget before the house. In the first place it will authorize the government to raise the necessary amount of money to carry on the war and to take care of all other governmental expenditures. I do not believe there is one hon. member in this house who will not agree with this particular feature of the budget, because we are providing the money necessary to carry on the war.
In the second place, by means of this budget the Minister of Finance will, in my opinion, induce many Canadian people to study the monetary reform economics more than anyone else has done for a long while, with the one exception, the greatest man in this field in Canada. I refer to the Hon. Mr. Aberhart, Premier of Alberta. The minister should be congratulated upon this, even though it was perhaps his intention to guard against this very thing.
In the third place the budget, by its very construction, underlines the faulty principles of the present outlived financial system. It is only six or seven days since this budget was brought down, but I have already been approached by a number of civil servants and a great number of members of this house, who in the past have been deaf to everything this group has said about monetary reform. The civil servant class have in the past been drifting from day to day; all they had to worry about was to adjust themselves to the new party when a new party came into office, but I believe this budget will wake them up. In fact, there is evidence of this already. I believe that many of the thinking and progressive people of Canada will from now on explore every feature of the monetary reform proposals that this group has been placing before the country for the past seven or eight years. I cannot believe' that the people of Canada will accept this budget in the best of spirits, even though I do not doubt their sincere willingness to carry the greatest of burdens in time of peace and much more so in time of war. But it seems to me that the financial institutions are taking advantage of the loyalty of our people. I mean to say that they are taking advantage of this weakest
moment in our entire history, in this the greatest crisis that the British people have ever faced, and through the medium of this budget they are saddling the people of Canada with a debt which, as it is predicted, will rise to the amount of twelve billion dollars before the war is over.
This document should not only be termed "a budget," "an orthodox budget," but it might as well be called a mortgage upon every man, woman and child in Canada for generations to come. I understand that a number of hon. members are anxious to have this debate close to-night. I would not hold up the closing of this debate at any cost if I felt that this budget pjovpjod eip SUM. uuqt ^uiEpodan ssaj ojoav stunt called the plebiscite. The debate on the plebiscite took three or four weeks and, in reality, it simply meant nothing, but this budget proposes to impose upon our people heavy taxes and a debt that they will carry for generations. So it seems to me that a measure of this kind should receive more consideration than it seems to be getting in this house.
One cannot fail to appreciate the efforts of the Minister of Finance to make the old cart, the old money system, keep on working, but I am afraid that his effort will result in bitter fruit for the people of Canada after this war is over. I am of the opinion that had the minister pursued a different course, he had a chance of becoming one of the greatest men in Canadian history. He has the makings of a great man; he has the ability. But at this moment, when this nation and, indeed, the entire British commonwealth of nations are faced with this great crisis in their history, the minister chooses to bring in a budget which places a mortgage upon the nation. He had an opportunity of scrapping this budget and, throwing it in the waste-paper basket; he could have brought in his own budget before this house and he could have told hon. members and the people of Canada that we have come to a point where the life of the nation is more important than all the financial considerations put together. Had he brought down a budget of that sort, I am sure the people of Canada would have supported him, and we would then have been sure to do our part in this crisis in a much better way than we may now be able to do.
I am afraid that it is the old financial system which has placed this nation and the rest of the British Commonwealth of Nations in the position in which we find ourselves to-day; and if we get any set-backs in the future, I believe it will be the fault, not of the people of the British Commonwealth of Nations, but of those who are in control of the financial system and
The Budget-Mr. Hlynka

be raised by loans. There will be raised by loan, $1,850,000,000 this year. This means that there will be imposed upon the people of Canada a mortgage of $1,850,000,000. In other words, as the hon. member who preceded me said, the war expenditure alone will cost the people of Canada $6,300 per minute or $23 per family per week, as compared with $16.80 per family per week last year.
Some hon. members and certainly members of the cabinet will say: "But we cannot possibly change from the present system in the middle of the stream, so we must continue with this borrowing and we will take care of everything when the war is over. After the war we will give the people a new deal." But how can they give the people of Canada a new deal, when they are using the same old deck of marked cards and the same old tricks are being employed? It may be a new deal, but, believe me, the common people of Canada will not be any better off.
