speechtext:
Yes. I should like to be optimistic and feel that this young nation of perhaps as fine a people as one can find anywhere in the world will emerge from this crisis to live comfortably in the future and build up a strong and a powerful nation. It is not merely a matter of getting by, because in the present world we must build a nation that will be powerful enough to compete with other nations, and be able to fight against them for its life. Unless we develop our resources, our aggressiveness, our educational capacities, and unless we are prepared to fight, we cannot possibly survive among the other nations of the world. We must either fight or die. That is the law of life, and we must realize it.
Before the war we could not distribute the goods of which we had an abundance, of which we had more than we ever needed for ourselves, because the financial system did not work, and now these same gentlemen come to us and tell us that they can take care of the money mechanism which controls the very lives of the people of this nation. They tell us they can carry along with the same old system and get us- through. But again I say I should like to feel optimistic about that.
This war should not place any debt burden whatsoever upon the people of Canada. The Prime Minister of Great Britain, Mr. Churchill, has spoken of "blood, sweat and tears," and he has written a book under the same title. He might have added "tiio
[Mr. Hlynka.1
material resources of the country." Beyond the blood, sweat and tears and the material resources of the country which are spent, this war should not cost the people of Canada anything. After the conclusion of the war, Canada should not owe a cent to anybody. This idea of telling the people of Canada, or of any other country for that matter, that they must be subjected to heavy taxation and the heaviest of debts-and we do not mind taxation as much as the debt-in order to pay for the war is all hay-wire. There is no need at all for this debt pyramid. Let me illustrate.
A farmer decides to build a log house for himself. He has all the logs on his own farm. He supplies his own labour. Perhaps he has to sell some of his farm produce in order to buy nails and shingles. Then, with everything necessary to build the log house, he goes ahead and completes it. After he has completed it, there is no reason in the world why he should owe anybody anything, having built it out of his own materials and by his own labour.
Similarly, the Dominion of Canada in this war is using her own natural resources, her own materials and her own labour, and with that she is building aeroplanes, ships and tanks. Yet every year we are going into debt. Why are we going into debt? What are we going into debt for? I should like to know. Of course, if we have to buy a certain amount of needed materials from the United States, we must pay for them, and in that one instance we would be incurring a small debt. But paying even for these things which we buy from the United States we pay with the exchange of goods. It follows, then, that the whole debt structure narrows down to an exchange of goods between the two countries in order that we could get the materials we require. Therefore there is no reason in the world why this government should be mortgaging the people of Canada to-day and the future generations for years to come.

Mr. LIGUORI LACOMBE (Laval-Two
Mountains) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, this budget clearly shows that the government is not deepely concerned about the difficulties experienced by our farmers in hiring the help they need. The government gives no indication of the means it intends to take in order to secure for agriculture the labour supply it needs. Agriculture feeds our armies and our civilian population, and it remains our first line of defence. What is the administration doing in order to maintain and stimulate that essential source of supply, that powerful factor so essential to the triumph of our arms? I cannot

The Budget-Mr. Lacombe
find in the entire budget a single resolution providing against the shortage of farm labour. I have searched in vain for such provision. How can we explain such indifference concerning a situation as alarming as the shortage of farm labour? Is the government blindly leading the country to decay, starvation and defeat? When will they open their eyes to the unfortunate lot of our farmers whose production is falling off daily and to such an extent that, in a country like ours, rationing even of farm produ ucts has already become necessary for the army and the civilian population? How often have we not pointed out to the government one of the essential duties they must fulfil, that of maintaining agriculture as our first line of defence? How often have we not urged them to stop calling up for military service young men whose labour is essential on the farm? It was a waste of time. However, no one can charge us with neglecting our duty in that connection.
There is another restriction which could easily have been avoided in Canada. I refer to the rationing of oil and gasoline. Our country's oil resources have scarcely been developed. Governments of every political stripe have shown the same lack of foresight in that respect. Why is it that our oil fields are almost untouched in many areas of the country? Who has prevented the development of such an asset as valuable in peace time as in war? We are reaping to-day the results of the culpable negligence of men whose prime duty was to ensure the development of our raw materials. And now the restrictions placed on oil and gasoline threaten the very life of our industries and our trade. They will soon affect our agriculture as well. The shipment of farm products will be greatly hindered by all those restrictions. Agriculture itself will be placed under a severe handicap. And has any thought been given to our mechanized army? The future is far from reassuring in that respect. Such are the reasons impelling me to vote against this motion.
I shall certainly not vote for this measure which is, on the whole, a challenge to the most elementary principles of political economy. Never in the history of Canada have taxpayers in the lower brackets been so cruelly and so unjustly burdened. Nor does the government give the slightest indication that it intends to prepare the people for this war's terrible aftermath? That is undoubtedly of importance to the administration at the moment. Such, however, is not our opinion, and we are determined to recall the government to reality as often as we deem it necessary. Before concluding my remarks, I shall move an amendment to the motion before the house.

speechtext:
You said it right over there. We have heard it several times, that he was too hasty in declaring war on Germany, Japan and Italy. But in years to come it will be said of the Prime Minister, even by his opponents, as was said of George Washington, that he was "first in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen."
I see the Social Credit party are amusing themselves. I did not have time to reply to the speech made by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka), but, Mr. Speaker, he put such physical energy and such convulsive effort into his speech that I was reminded of John Hay's description of a steamboat which he once saw stranded on the shoals of one of the great lakes. He said:
She hove and set and hove and set And high her rudder flung;
And every time she hove and set The worser leak she sprung.
The leader of the opposition has spoken of two great statesmen, but when the history of this country comes to be written the names of two other great statesmen will be closely linked in connection with responsible government in Canada. First, I refer to the name of William Lyon Mackenzie, who fought and suffered for responsible government in Canada and afterwards sat in a duly elected parliament ; and second, sir, I refer to his illustrious namesake and grandson, the present Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King), who has spent the greater part of his life in seeking to maintain and improve responsible government in Canada.
We are told that we should have a national government in Canada, and that then everything will be peaceful and harmonious. What is the state of affairs in Britain to-day, where they have a national government? Are they not every day asking the Prime Minister of England to resign, and offering votes of want of confidence in him? Of course, we all want to win the war, and I believe we shall. But let us not depend upon Providence; let us not depend upon the slogan that England always wins the last battle. In the words of John Bright, as nearly as I can remember, I would say, "Let us not lay all our difficulties at the door of Providence; man must do his part". We must do our part. We must retrace our steps; we must shun the blunders.

The Budget-Speaker's Ruling
and then and not until then we shall see in this country an enduring edifice of victory and peace.

I have been considering the amendment moved by the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe), which was:
That all the words after the word "that" in the motion be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"This house is of the opinion that, owing to the difficulties experienced by farmers in securing farm hands, the food production will be decreased as a consequence of the compulsory service to such an extent as to endanger the victory of the nations who are fighting the axis powers."
This amendment is on the same lines as the amendment which I have already ruled out of order this evening. It is an amendment which cannot be moved on going into committee of ways and means; it is a substantive motion, and it has no bearing upon or relevancy to the question before the house.
I also think this amendment is subject to the same objection which was taken to the former amendment, namely that the amendment moved by the hon, member is along lines similar to the notice of motion which appears on the order paper in his name, and which reads as follows:
Mr. Lacombe-The following proposed resolution: Whereas agriculture is essential to the upkeep of the armies and the welfare of the civil population.
Therefore be it resolved: That, in the opinion of this house, farmers, farm employees and all persons engaged in industries connected with agriculture or with war industries, should be exempt from military service and that exemption tribunals should be set up in each constituency in the country to investigate each case on its merits.
The same subject matter is contained in that notice of motion, and in accordance with the rules of the house already quoted- Beauchesne, citation No. 398; May, 13th edition, pages S25 and 526, and Bourinot, page 420-I must rule the amendment out of order.

[Mr. Grant.l

Motion agreed to.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): I intend to be very brief, Mr. Speaker. I am sure every hon. member will join in applause when I say that the mantle of Ulysses Grant has evidently fallen upon the shoulders of his namesake who has just spoken in this debate.
This is a budget so considerable in scope, sir, that it deserves close study, and it is impossible to say in a few words all we have to say in a debate such as this. Everyone realizes that with the country at war we have to assume obligations that are out of the ordinary; but when we are told that we must bear sacrifices it should be understood that the sacrifices which are made or are to be made must always be useful to the community. It was said again and again during and after the last war that one-third of the moneys voted for that war was stolen, one-third was wasted and only one-third was spent for real war purposes. At that time there were detailed estimates and public accounts. At the present time there are no detailed estimates, and the public accounts give very little information. I complained about this situation last year and was promised that there would be an improvement. There was none. I was told by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) that the limit below which the details were not given was $35,000. Later this statement was corrected by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley), who said that items of less than $25,000 were not appearing in the public accounts.	*
This is an abnormal situation, and the war is not an excuse for it. Even if no one reads the public accounts from the first line to the last, they provide security for the state in that the figures are given to the public, and everyone has an opportunity to learn what is being done with regard to the spending of public money. Recently I read an article which appeared in the Monetary Times of May 30 of this year, the title of which might be taken as the text of the few remarks I have to make:
When Deceit is a Virtue
The art of camouflage flourishes during war time until it becomes exotic trickery, flinging

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot
the cloak of invisibility over once visible objects. It is as ancient as war itself and just as difficult.
We live in times when things are not called by their own names. It seems there has been a shake-up of the dictionary, and it is most difficult for any one of us to know exactly what is going on behind the curtain. Members of parliament are not consulted; their advice is not sought before policies of great importance are drafted and submitted to this house. We have the feeling of doing nothing, while we are willing to do our very best to help the government; and those who are substituted for us are men without contact with the people, men whose heads are filled with theories that may bring this country to disaster. I remember that the day after the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announced that this country was to make a gift to Great Britain of a thousand million dollars, a dispatch appeared in either the morning or the afternoon newspapers to the effect that the news had been received very coldly in Great Britain. It was only after this that the newspapers published the cablegram which was sent by Mr. Churchill.
That is not all, sir. It is the poor who have to pay to the rich. This was the policy enunciated by Mr. Bennett, who thought those who should be taxed were not the rich but the poor, in order to make them realize the importance of raising public money and of taxation in government business.
That gift of one billion dollars is an absurdity. There is no precedent for it. I have no objection to helping Great Britain, but why do we not have a recognition of that gift? It would have put Great Britain to no embarrassment, and it would have given us an opportunity to discuss peace with Great Britain and the other countries on business terms. I should like to quote from the great English financial weekly, The Economist, of April 25, 1942. A report from their Ottawa correspondent, dated March 19, reads:
At the present rate of British procurement in Canada, this sum will last for something less than twelve months. An extension of the gift policy can be foreseen when the amount is exhausted, unless in the meantime an arrangement by which pooling of production surpluses of the united nations is then in operation. Conceivably, the Canadian surplus might then be pooled and drawn on by the United Kingdom and other allies under terms not yet executed. Other heavy customers of Canadian war materials at present are Egypt, India and Australia in the sterling area and Russia and China outside it. The new Canadian proposal is designed to avoid the growth of an unmanageable war debt between Canada and Britain. Logically it should apply to other allies who share access to Canadian war output. There is
a growing sentiment at Ottawa that an allied pooling arrangement should be effected speedily. Negotiations with Washington and London are leading to some such arrangement.
It is a yearly instalment, and we shall have to expect more of that absurd policy. It is suggested that it should be extended to other countries. Have we the means to do that? My answer is "no." What was the purpose of doing it? It was to redeem securities held in Great Britain. I should like to remind the house of what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) said on March 20, 1941, as reported on pages 1868 and 1869 of Hansard. He said:
My hon. friend-
That was myself.
-refers to Sir Edward Peacock and to the mission on which he is engaged in the United States. There has been no suggestion that his mission will be extended to Canada, nor have I any expectation that it will be so extended.
In the Montreal Gazette of June 25 I noted that the great financier, Sir Edward Peacock, was here along with Sir Arthur Salter; that both were at the Ritz Carlton in Montreal. A number of questions asked by me were answered in return No. 290 of May 23. The question I asked was:
Did Sir Edward Peacock come to Canada on or about June 25, 1941? If so, did the Honourable Minister of Finance meet him? If not, was he met by other members of the cabinet?
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) reported no information. The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) reported that Sir Edward Peacock was met by the minister himself. I would not be surprised if the Minister of Munitions and Supply met Sir Edward Peacock when he was in the United States and when he was doing some business with him regarding the amalgamation of the railways.

The answer is given by Mr. Sheils, the deputy. I asked:
Did Sir Edward Peacock come to Canada on or about June 25, 1941?
And the department answered "yes". My next question was:
If so, did the Honourable Minister of Finance meet him?
The answer given was:
To be answered elsewhere.
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot

The next question was:
If not, was he met by other members of the cabinet ?
The answer given was:
Yes, by the Minister of Munitions and Supply.
Did Sir Edward Peacock come to Canada just to meet the Minister of Munitions and Supply and say, "how do you do?", and hear him say in reply "how do you do?" When I asked if Sir Edward Peacock would come here, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) told me that he did not believe he would, and yet we have the statement that the Minister of Munitions and Supply met him. That statement is more authoritative than hearsay evidence from the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance cannot speak from his own personal knowledge because he was not in Ottawa at the time.

The Department of National Defence is the most important department in this war, and I do not see how the Minister of National Defence has the spare time to look after the Department of Finance, the wartime prices and trade
[Mr. Pouliot.l
board, and all the other things that come under the finance department. There is something else I should like to ask the minister. If he likes he may answer me after I am through, or he can take a note of it. How is it that the Minister of National Defence was appointed Acting Minister of Finance precisely at the time when Sir Edward Peacock was in Montreal?

Lord Mottistone said he had made the suggestion to a Canadian officer with a distinguished record, who had replied, "that just suits me".
He was introducing a motion in the upper house asking the government to take prompt action to increase the offensive power and equipment of the citizens of Britain. Equipment had been greatly increased, he declared, but the method of meeting an invasion needed more consideration.
This was said by Lord Mottistone. What did Herbert Morrison say in London? It is reported in the morning press of July 1. I have a Quebec paper in my hand, I do not have an English clipping; but this is what Mr. Morrison stated:
He declared that if a second front is opened it will be the Canadian troops who will constitute the spearhead of the allied armies that are to invade Europe.
The word "spearhead" is just the expression which was used by General Crerar a month and a half ago. .
I was very sorry to read in the press yesterday and to-day what the Prime Minister said in the house. It was a hint that the time for action in Europe was closer for the forces of Canada. Plenty of water has been running under the mill from July 3, 1940 to July 1, 1942. Now we see the effect of the propaganda which has been made by paid agents with this government and other influential people to induce them to forget that Canada is their country, and to put to shame Canadians who desire to stress the necessity of defending this country. We have the lesson of all other countries in the world, and I find it most illogical that the nearer the danger is to us the more men are sent overseas. What was the solemn promise which was made to the British government by the Minister of National Defence in the first winter of the war? He never told this house. I asked him once, and he did not answer me; he just mentioned a promise, without telling what it was, at a meeting which was held in the committee room, after the adjournment of one of the sessions, and at which were present the two hon. members for Ottawa. But we as members of the House of Commons had no details about it. At that time the number of recruits that were to be called up was only one-half of the number that we have now. Therefore I wonder whether a second promise has not been made by some member of the government to send all our men overseas and to keep nobody here to defend this country or to operate war industry. Can you expect, sir, men coming-out of the Lady Grey hospital here in Ottawa, 
sufferers from tuberculosis, or from the Lake Edward sanatorium in the province of Quebec, to act as brakemen or firemen on the railways? Railways are a war industry. That was admitted by the Minister of National Defence himself in the railways and shipping committee. Therefore, sir, that work should be done by men who are fit, and this is the more necessary because of the tremendous amount of traffic that we have now. What about the other industries in which we need able-bodied men to do work which is to help the army as well as the civilian population? But this, sir, does not count. You cannot put men who suffer from tuberculosis, men over the military age, men unfit for military service, in these very responsible positions. And this is the idea of sacrifice ! One day I said that the "Isaac" atmosphere of sacrifice was all wrong; and the reporter put "Isis", but that is not what I said. We should not consider these matters from the sentimental point of view. Everything should be reasoned precisely in war time. Military science is just the application of common sense to the realities of life.
What I fear, is not what is done openly but what is under camouflage, what is hidden because one is afraid of telling "the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth" to the Canadian people, who deserve to hear nothing than that.	[DOT]
I regret that I am very miserable in the house since I have lost a very dear friend, one who was most unselfish, who was a friend of every hon. member and the sanest adviser the Prime Minister ever had. At times I did not agree with him on certain matters, but it was possible to discuss things with him, although I did not abuse the privilege. He was a big brother to me, and he was the right hand of the Prime Minister. I know the Prime Minister feels his loss very deeply. He will remember also that during the Christmas season when he went to Washington to meet Mr. Churchill as well as President Roosevelt, I sent him a telegram of good wishes, and I added to it, "Please, sir, when you get to Washington do not forget the memory of Ernest Lapointe, who was your best friend as well as mine." There is a saying to the effect that the dead go fast, but in my view, sir, if Mr. Lapointe had been alive, there are many difficulties which we would not now have to face.
There is another thing that I want to say. At home I have a picture of the first cabinet of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, taken in the council room, and on the wall there is a painting representing Our Lord among the doctors of law in the temple. I wonder if that painting

The Budget-Division
is still there or if it has been removed. At any rate, it was an inspiration for the ministers of the day to have a reminder of Christian ideals while they were discussing national problems. I hope that if the picture is not there, the idea which it portrays has not been forgotten, and that in all the policies that are to be submitted to this house the first consideration will be, not of any other country, but of Canada first. I have never said this so loud, but it is time now to come down to earth. What is the difference between a statesman and a politician? A statesman is such a great man that his head is above the clouds and he does not see what happens on the earth; a politician is a smaller man, with his head under the clouds, who sees what is going on. I suggest to the ministers that they be not influenced by the flattery of interested men who want jobs, contracts or favours. Let them not forget that quotation from the scriptures that "the wounds of those who love are better than the kisses of those who hate".

LAURENT: As a matter of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I wish to state for the information of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) that I was for a few months a member of the board of directors of the bank of Montreal; that I resigned therefrom when I became a member of this government; that I never at any time discussed any matter, relating directly or indirectly to amalgamation of the Canadian railways, with anyone connected with the bank of Montreal, nor did I at any time hear any matter, relating directly or indirectly to any such amalgamation, discussed by any person connected in any way with the bank of Montreal.
